sources.title: Jake Castillo on scaling Cal AI to $40M ARR: UGC, influencers, paid ads, pricing and hiring
sources.originalTitle: Cal AI's $40M ARR | Jake Castillo on the Truth About Scaling Apps in 2026
sources.summary: Jake Castillo, Cal AI's CMO and COO, explains how Cal AI reached 15M users and $40M ARR in 18 months. He covers niching down, choosing between UGC, influencers and paid ads by cash position, running about 300 paywall tests, pricing, LTV, and hiring hungry people.

principles.text: Saturation isn't a barrier: win with a novel feature that removes friction, not a clone of incumbents.
principles.quote: if you have a product that has a novel feature and that feature is better than what's currently in the market, I I don't think you have to worry about saturation

principles.text: In a crowded category, niche down to a specific audience; niche drives the marketing angle, then the UI.
principles.quote: you start with the you start with the niche, then you go with the marketing angle, and then you can create your UI.

principles.text: UGC is a swing at the algorithm: pay flat fees, absorb risk upfront, and capture viral upside.
principles.quote: Pay flat fees. Absorb that risk upfront so you can capture the upside when it does eventually go viral.

principles.text: Vet creators by their comment section; real conversations signal real influence and can't be faked.
principles.quote: I you can't fake the comment section.

principles.text: Pick the channel by cash position: UGC if broke, influencers with some budget, paid ads once cash flow isn't a concern.
principles.quote: If like cash flow is not a concern, I think paid ads is a good place to play. If you are tight on money, I think UGC is the place to play

principles.text: LTV is what lets you outspend competitors on acquisition, so keep testing paywalls constantly.
principles.quote: It's the only way you will be able to durably win is if you can acquire customers at a higher cost than your competitors.

sources.title: How Cal AI turned creators into a growth machine: the magic moment test, RPM caps, and flat-rate deals
sources.originalTitle: How Cal AI turned creators into a growth machine — Jake Castillo, Cal AI
sources.summary: Jake Castillo, Cal AI co-founder, explains how the team scaled via fitness creators: picking niches whose audiences actually want the product, structuring deals around RPM, and layering paid ads on top. He covers the magic moment test, reading comments instead of views, low-price strategy, and doing unglamorous outreach for 18 months.

principles.text: Views and followers can lie, but comments can't. Check comment sections to validate niche and individual creator fit.
principles.quote: views can lie, followers can lie, but comments cannot, right? The truth is always in the comments.

principles.text: Creator-led distribution needs a magic moment: instantly understandable, double-take-worthy, no long explanation, or it feels like an ad.
principles.quote: If your app doesn't have a magic moment, it doesn't lend itself well to a seamless integration because it's not going to cause that double take.

principles.text: Never pay a CPM above your revenue per thousand views; that is the hard cap on what you can pay creators.
principles.quote: you can't pay like a CPM that is higher than that RPM otherwise like you are guaranteed to not be profitable right like it's just math

principles.text: Prefer flat-rate deals so you capture the asymmetric upside of viral hits; break-even is set on average views.
principles.quote: if you're not doing flat rates it makes it hard to capture that asymmetric upside that is a viral hit.

principles.text: A cult-like following is a lagging indicator. Sign promising creators early on cheaper deals and ride their growth, with personal relationships and bonuses.
principles.quote: a cult-like following is a lagging indicator. If you're a great creator, the cultlike following will come.

principles.text: Use organic creator content for subtle integrations and dedicated paid creative with a hard sell; hook must relate to the product, and ad, store and onboarding must be congruent.
principles.quote: where we really started to see results is when we invested in dedicated paid ad creative.

sources.title: How Cal AI scaled with influencer and UGC marketing: Jake Castillo's playbook
sources.originalTitle: Cal AI’s Co-Founder Shares His App Growth Secrets
sources.summary: Jake Castillo explains how Cal AI grew by signing hundreds of health and fitness creators who scan food on camera. He covers creator selection by views, CPM versus RPM math, capped view bonuses, UGC economics, and constant testing.

principles.text: Let influencers make their normal content and slide your app into it; don't force a format.
principles.quote: you get these creators making their normal content and just like sliding your app into that.

principles.text: Price by views, not followers. Judge creators by average views, using a worst-case average.
principles.quote: Followers means nothing to me. What matters is how many views they get on average per video.

principles.text: CPM doesn't matter in itself; keep it below your revenue per thousand views (RPM).
principles.quote: the CPM doesn't matter. All that matters is that your CPM is lower than your RPM.

principles.text: Cap view bonuses (around 1M views); UGC profit comes from the rare viral hit, and later views convert worse.
principles.quote: you want to cap it at a certain point. That way, like everything past that is just gravy for you.

principles.text: Always be testing, but adapt general principles to your product; don't copy another app's exact numbers.
principles.quote: what works for my app will may not work for your app and what works for your app may not work for my app.

principles.text: Run a high risk tolerance; big bets give asymmetric payouts, and scale outreach with systems and automation.
principles.quote: you should have an incredibly high risk tolerance because like it's taking those big bets that's going to have the asymmetric payout.

sources.title: Jake Castillo: UGC creator playbook that took Cal AI to 15M users (zero to $10K/month)
sources.originalTitle: I Built A $30M iOS App: This is My Growth Playbook
sources.summary: Jake Castillo, former CMO of Cal AI, lays out a five-step UGC creator system for taking an app from zero to $10K/month: source talking-head creators, warm up dedicated accounts, pick a content format (magic moment vs painful problem), run RPM vs CPM economics, then cut and scale creators. Includes concrete pricing, benchmarks and ratios.

principles.text: Good outputs start with great inputs; creators are your inputs, and weak on-camera talent breaks the whole system.
principles.quote: good outputs start with great inputs and creators are your inputs. You can have the best scripts and the best app in the world, but if the person delivering the content isn't compelling, it's impossible to make the system work.

principles.text: Small teams should use UGC creators on brand-new dedicated accounts instead of paying expensive large influencers.
principles.quote: For a small startup or solo founder, paying large influencers can get very expensive. That's why I really like UGC.

principles.text: Test creators cheaply first (10 videos at $10), then move proven ones to a full campaign with view bonuses.
principles.quote: I'm talking like 10 test videos at $10 a video. And if those videos are good, then you can extend them to like a full campaign where it's 30 videos a month at $30 per video

principles.text: Warm up creator accounts and prove they aren't shadowbanned before posting branded content.
principles.quote: And then once you see a video breaks a thousand views, you can have them start posting actual branded content.

principles.text: Pick content format by asking: magic moment means maximize views; else a painful problem means maximize intent; else rethink the product.
principles.quote: The first question you got to ask is does my app have a magic moment? And by magic moment, I mean a feature that is so visually impressive that if someone sees it on screen, they're going to do almost like a double take.

principles.text: Judge creators by revenue per 1,000 views against what you paid per 1,000 views, and scale when RPM clearly beats CPM.
principles.quote: if I'm paying a $1.50 to acquire a customer that pays me $4, then I'm ready to scale.

sources.title: How Cal AI hit $50M ARR: influencer integrations, creator vetting, and relentless volume
sources.originalTitle: Cal AI grew to $50m ARR. Their co-founder told me how they did it:
sources.summary: Jake Castillo, Cal AI co-founder, explains the bootstrapped influencer-marketing playbook behind Cal AI's growth to $50M ARR and the My Fitness Pal exit. He covers replicating winning creator formats, vetting creators in seconds, writing outreach DMs, paying upfront, and the work ethic required.

principles.text: When a creative format works, replicate it relentlessly across creators and niches until it stops working.
principles.quote: when you see something that works like don't try and reinvent the wheel. Just try and replicate and do it over and over until it stops working and hopefully it never does.

principles.text: Make the sponsored post look like the creator's normal content so your floor equals their average views.
principles.quote: You need your floor to be their average number of views so that potentially you could get the ceiling that is like that outlier that's extremely successful

principles.text: If your product is easy to understand and has a magic moment, use seamless integrations; otherwise use a hard sell.
principles.quote: Do I have a product that's like easy to understand and a product that has a magic moment? If the answer to both of those things is yes, then you don't need to do like a hard sell in the integration.

principles.text: Vet creators fast: sufficient views, real comments and reply threads, and talking-to-audience content that signals a cult-like following.
principles.quote: which essentially what you're finding out there is like which influencer has a cult-like following. And when you see like really good comments, that's a good indicator of a cultlike following.

principles.text: Write short outreach DMs that lead with 'paid promo' so they catch the eye in the inbox preview and are easy to answer.
principles.quote: Don't tell them your life story... just say like paid promo like I want to pay you money like let me pay you.

principles.text: Pay creators upfront to remove their risk of being burned by sketchy brands.
principles.quote: I'm eliminating all that risk for you. I'm paying you upfront. I'm the one taking the bet on you.

sources.title: 34 truths on scaling consumer apps, from Cal AI's $50M ARR run
sources.originalTitle: 34 Truths Nobody Tells You About Scaling Consumer Apps
sources.summary: Jake Castillo, who ran marketing and operations at Cal AI from zero to $50M ARR in about 18 months, lists 34 operator lessons. Themes: diagnose the funnel constraint before adding traffic, price creators on total cost and variance, keep features and retention loops tied to core value, and treat execution volume as the real moat.

principles.text: Find where the funnel is broken (distribution, creative, onboarding, offer) before chasing more users.
principles.quote: More traffic poured into a broken funnel just helps you lose faster.

principles.text: Weak paywall conversion often traces back to the ad, store page or onboarding; the paywall just reveals it.
principles.quote: The lie may have started in the ad, the App Store page or the onboarding.

principles.text: Consumer apps should prioritize acquisition; B2B SaaS prioritizes reliability and retention. Don't import SaaS playbooks.
principles.quote: Stop importing B2B SaaS playbooks into consumer and wondering why the math doesn’t work.

principles.text: Improve retention by making the action retained users already repeat faster, clearer and more valuable, not by adding features.
principles.quote: Find the action retained users already repeat, then simply:

principles.text: Creator cost includes management time, so a cheap-fee creator can cost more than a pricier one.
principles.quote: Creator CAC includes management bandwidth, so price it that way.

principles.text: A visible tactic isn't a moat; relentless daily execution volume is.
principles.quote: Information is easy to copy, but sustained execution volume is not.

sources.title: 8 uncomfortable truths about consumer apps in 2026: moats, retention, checkout and experiment velocity
sources.originalTitle: 8 Uncomfortable Truths About Consumer Apps In 2026
sources.summary: Jake Castillo synthesizes RevenueCat, Adapty and AppsFlyer research to argue consumer apps are easier to build but harder to win. AI moved the moat to distribution, brand, retention and experiment speed; first-session activation, channel ecosystems, web checkout tradeoffs and iOS vs Android differences decide who wins.

principles.text: When AI makes features copyable in days, the moat is distribution, brand, creators, data, trust, experiment velocity and retention.
principles.quote: The moat moved into everything surrounding the product:

principles.text: A good product without a repeatable way to reach customers is a side project waiting to be copied, so distribution beats product.
principles.quote: a good product with no repeatable way to reach customers is not a real business, it’s really just a side project waiting to be copied.

principles.text: Sell the outcome, not the AI. AI converts well but retains worse, so the customer outcome is the real product.
principles.quote: AI is the mechanism, and the outcome is the real product.

principles.text: Use organic as the testing ground, then put paid spend behind winning concepts and formats; evaluate channels as one ecosystem.
principles.quote: Organic is a great testing ground, and then paid is where you put spend behind your winning concepts and formats to fuel sustainable and predictable growth.

principles.text: Skip the product tour: get users to the magic moment, then present the offer in context of the result they just experienced.
principles.quote: It gets the user to the magic moment, then puts the offer in context of the result they just experienced.

principles.text: Margin saved is not revenue earned: web checkout can cut fees but add friction, so test it by audience.
principles.quote: It means margin saved is not the same as revenue earned.

sources.title: Free trial length: why longer trials convert but shorter ones buy attribution (Cal AI)
sources.originalTitle: Free Trial Trivia - what length is best?
sources.summary: Jake Castillo explains how to choose free trial length and whether to go freemium. Longer trials convert better because people forget to cancel, but shorter trials give clean install-to-revenue attribution when buying traffic through creators. Freemium only works when the free feature differs from the paid upsells.

principles.text: Run free trials only after proof of PMF; trials can't fix a boring product or bad messaging.
principles.quote: Free trials can be a part of any consumer app growth strategy, but only after you have significant proof that people actually want your product and will pay for it.

principles.text: Longer trials convert better because users forget to cancel, which also helps recoup ad spend.
principles.quote: So yes, longer trials convert better because you’re banking on subscribers forgetting to cancel.

principles.text: Short trials trigger immediate cancellations; most 3-day cancels happen on day 0 or 1.
principles.quote: According to RevenueCat, 84% of 3-day trial cancellations happen on day 0 or day 1.

principles.text: Every extra trial day adds noise between install and charge, hurting creator attribution.
principles.quote: Every day you add to your trial is another day of variables between the install and when their credit card gets charged.

principles.text: Attribution matters more than conversion rate when deciding which creators to keep, since audiences differ in paying power.
principles.quote: attribution is how you decide who to keep or cut on your roster of creators.

principles.text: Not paying for traffic: go long. Buying installs: shorten, since trial length is the price of signal.
principles.quote: You're not optimizing conversion at that point, you're buying signal, and trial length is what you pay for it.

sources.title: Influencer marketing still works, it just stopped being cheap: why UGC is the window
sources.originalTitle: Will Influencer Marketing ACTUALLY Work For Me??
sources.summary: Jake argues influencer marketing still works but CPMs have spiked across all creator tiers because everyone copied the Cal AI playbook, killing margins. He recommends shifting to UGC (not yet exhausted or overpriced), sourcing via SideShift or Trybe, and moving Q4 effort into organic since paid CPMs spike. He lists funnel prerequisites UGC needs to convert.

principles.text: Influencer marketing still works; the problem is price. CPMs rose while creator quality and RPMs stayed flat.
principles.quote: Influencer marketing didn't stop working. It just stopped being cheap.

principles.text: When a profitable playbook gets copied, everyone bids for the same creators and creators reprice, killing margins.
principles.quote: People saw what we were doing (and other profitable brands too) to scale our operations and decided influencer marketing was the move.

principles.text: Move into the channel that isn't yet exhausted or overpriced. UGC is where influencer marketing was a couple of years ago.
principles.quote: UGC hasn't been exhausted YET and it's not overpriced YET.

principles.text: Source UGC creators via performance-based pay (Trybe) or abundant supply (SideShift), plus a VA doing manual outreach.
principles.quote: Creators make the content with nothing paid upfront, you run it as an ad, and they take a percentage of the spend on the video they made (you pay out only on performance).

principles.text: Don't try to outbid in Q4 paid ads; accept slower paid scaling for consumer apps and invest in organic channels.
principles.quote: My advice is to not try to outbid anybody.

principles.text: UGC only works if fundamentals are in place: angles, scripts, a product understood in seconds, test budget, and an optimized funnel.
principles.quote: If your product is hard to understand in 2-5 seconds

sources.title: Build for the silent majority: why to ignore power users and the loud minority (Cal AI's Android mistake)
sources.originalTitle: Timeless lessons in building apps the right way
sources.summary: Jake Castillo argues founders sample feedback from the groups that talk (power users via behavior, complainers via support channels) while the silent majority generates most revenue. Using a mass-market gym analogy and Cal AI's Android launch, he says to build for the majority, simplify the first screen, and sanity-check requests with three numbers.

principles.text: Founders are power users of their own product, a costly bias in consumer apps.
principles.quote: Every founder I know is a power user of their own product.

principles.text: Usually ignore or delay off-the-wall requests from a loud minority; they are a misleading demand signal.
principles.quote: That is usually a misleading demand signal, and most of the time you should ignore or delay building any of the off-the-wall requests you get from users.

principles.text: Build for the majority of basic users first, not the power-user minority, like mass-market gyms do.
principles.quote: you should always be building apps for the majority first, not the minority.

principles.text: A big market-size number can attach to the wrong population: Android's 70% wasn't addressable, so Cal AI grew maybe 10%.
principles.quote: So the 70% was never addressable. It was a real number attached to the wrong population.

principles.text: Your loudest signals and your biggest revenue segment are almost always different people.
principles.quote: Your loudest signals and your biggest revenue segment are 99% of the time two different groups of people.

principles.text: Before building a requested feature, write down how many asked, what share would pay, and what share of the silent majority would use it.
principles.quote: before you build the next thing everybody is asking for, write down three numbers:

sources.title: The Cautious Tale of Cal AI: luck, headhunters, and hiring for availability and learning
sources.originalTitle: The Cautious Tale Of Cal AI
sources.summary: Jake Castillo says Cal AI's rise to #1 in Health & Fitness and $50M ARR in eighteen months owed a lot to luck, not a replicable process. His practical advice: pay for great talent via headhunters, sell candidates hard, give generous equity, and hire for availability and ability to learn over experience.

principles.text: Luck plays a big role in winning; hard work and smarts mainly increase your surface area for luck.
principles.quote: Working hard and being smart just increases your surface area for luck.

principles.text: Don't wait to assemble a perfect, once-in-a-lifetime founding team; you may die waiting.
principles.quote: So if you are sitting there waiting to assemble a group of once-in-a-lifetime, Avengers style co-founders who happen to be brilliant AND happen to get along AND happen to be available, you might die waiting.

principles.text: Great talent is expensive and has options, so you have to pay to play.
principles.quote: Great people are expensive, hard to find, and already have options.

principles.text: Use a headhunter (about 20% of first-year salary) to source top talent fast; most founders are bad at sourcing.
principles.quote: Their fees usually cost around 20% of first-year salary and it is 100% worth it, because sourcing great talent is mind-numbing work and most founders have not hired enough people to be any good at it.

principles.text: Sell strong candidates hard on joining, since the best people don't need you, and be generous with equity.
principles.quote: you have to sell them hard on why they should work with you, because the person you want does not usually need you.

principles.text: Hire for availability and ability to learn rather than experience alone; experience can work against you.
principles.quote: Is this person actually here, and can they figure out something they do not currently know?

sources.title: Cal AI influencer playbook: how Jake Castillo scaled creator marketing, from vetting to outreach to payment
sources.originalTitle: I Exposed The Entire Cal AI Playbook On A Podcast
sources.summary: Jake Castillo distills eight tactics from the Cal AI creator-marketing playbook: price deals off average views, decide between soft and hard sell, target oversupplied creator niches, vet creators in 20 seconds, write short outreach, pay upfront, and repeat winning formats. He closes with the point that volume and relentless work, not a secret unlock, drove the results.

principles.text: Price creator deals off their average views, because sponsored posts usually underperform their normal content.
principles.quote: Almost every time, they're the sponsored posts. That happens because the brand made them deviate from what they normally do with their content. We priced every deal off a creator's average views, and you should too.

principles.text: If your product is easy to understand and has a magic moment, do a seamless integration; otherwise use a hard sell.
principles.quote: when your product has both, you can do a seamless integration and let the product carry the promo. But if you're missing either one, you need a hard sell.

principles.text: Go where creators outnumber brands to get cheaper deals; college students are an underserved supply.
principles.quote: Fitness worked partly because there are far more fitness creators than there are brands that are trying to work with them.

principles.text: Vet creators fast: 25k+ views, real comments, reply threads, and a parasocial bond signal a community that converts.
principles.quote: Reply threads mean the audience talks to each other, not just to the creator. That's a community, and communities convert better than anything else.

principles.text: Management time per creator is the same regardless of size, so spend your bandwidth on bigger creators.
principles.quote: A creator doing 20k views and a creator doing a million views cost you identical management time.

principles.text: Lead cold outreach with what's in it for them, keep it one-line answerable, and tailor price disclosure to creator experience.
principles.quote: don't open with your life story or how you're a bootstrapped founder, open with "paid promo" or something that answers the question, “What’s in it for me?”

sources.title: Learn app growth from seven operators actually shipping: who to follow and why
sources.originalTitle: 7 underrated app killers you need to know
sources.summary: Jake curates seven mobile app and subscription operators worth studying instead of courses or YouTube. He highlights concrete growth lessons: content-led distribution, ASO concentration on a few keywords, portfolio-of-simple-apps systems, and solo AI-assisted building.

principles.text: Learn from operators actively shipping and posting what works, not from courses or tutorial binges.
principles.quote: study these seven people who are _actually in the arena_, shipping apps, running profitable companies, and posting what works in real time.

principles.text: Write content that answers the exact questions your buyers are already Googling; it's a powerful distribution engine.
principles.quote: He grew it from $400/month to $2M ARR by writing content that answered the exact questions developers were Googling (an elite distribution lesson in itself).

principles.text: In paid search, downloads concentrate in a handful of keywords, so don't spread effort across hundreds.
principles.quote: even when you target hundreds of keywords in Apple Search Ads, most of your downloads come from just five to ten of them.

principles.text: You don't need a blockbuster app; a repeatable system of simple apps optimized for App Store discovery can win.
principles.quote: His entire approach is a repeatable system: find a niche, build simply, optimize for App Store discovery, and repeat.

principles.text: One person with AI tools and business sense can now build a real company with a tiny team.
principles.quote: one person with AI tools and business sense can build a real company.

principles.text: Onboarding and the early user experience determine whether someone churns or becomes a paying subscriber.
principles.quote: His specialty is onboarding and the early user experience, the exact moments that determine whether someone churns or becomes a paying subscriber.

sources.title: How to steal ecom retention playbooks (AG1, Olipop, BREZ) for your app
sources.originalTitle: How to become an app retention gangster
sources.summary: App founders echo-chamber on other app founders, but ecom brands have battle-tested retention playbooks because rising CAC forces them to preserve every customer. Jake says to take ecom principles (default subscription, lifecycle email, preservation vs generation) and translate them into app versions like paywall defaults and pause-instead-of-cancel.

principles.text: Look outside app land for retention ideas; ecom operators have the most battle-tested playbooks.
principles.quote: You need to start paying attention to the ecom bros.

principles.text: When acquisition costs climb, every funnel step matters; apps are heading to the same place as ecom.
principles.quote: When it costs that much to get a customer, every single step of their funnels matter.

principles.text: Make the annual plan the obvious paywall default instead of making users do math across plans.
principles.quote: Is the annual plan the obvious default?

principles.text: Split the business into generation (ads, content) and preservation (email, community) and staff preservation seriously.
principles.quote: Most app founders I talk to have a full team focused on generation and one intern fumbling around trying to keep customers from leaving..

principles.text: Treat subscription as a stage in the relationship: remove friction first, then add flexibility to avoid cancels.
principles.quote: His rule of thumb: remove the friction first, then add flexibility.

principles.text: Steal the principle, not the tactic, and translate it to an app version (pause instead of cancel, push before the habit breaks).
principles.quote: "Cancellation save offer" becomes "pause instead of cancel" in your manage-subscription flow.

sources.title: Influencer marketing tier list: why mid-level creators beat nano, big and celebrity creators
sources.originalTitle: The ultimate cheat sheet: influencer marketing edition
sources.summary: Jake Castillo ranks influencer tiers by conversion value, drawing on his experience at Cal AI and 10,000+ evaluated influencers. Mid-level creators are the best bet because deals still matter to them and audience trust is intact, while celebrities have no borrowed trust left to sell. He stresses per-deal effort and volume pipelines.

principles.text: Influencer programs hinge on two things: picking the right niche and finding creators with audiences primed to convert.
principles.quote: What makes or breaks any influencer marketing program is the ability to execute TWO tasks at a high level:

principles.text: Mid-level creators are the best tier: real reach, reasonable pricing, and trust still intact because nobody fights over them.
principles.quote: Nobody fights over these creators, because the giant brands chase celebrities and small brands chase micro-influencers, so partnership pricing stays reasonable.

principles.text: Even at the best tier you must run enough deals to find your winning formula; winners pay for the misses.
principles.quote: Our most profitable deals usually came from this level, and the winners paid for every deal that didn't hit.

principles.text: Micro-influencers work as a volume play, so build a pipeline that signs and manages dozens without hours of manual logistics.
principles.quote: This tier works as a volume play, which means you need a pipeline that signs and manages dozens of them without you spending hours managing all the logistics.

principles.text: Deal overhead is the same regardless of creator size, so nano deals can lose money; skip them unless effort per deal is near zero.
principles.quote: If you can't get this tier down to near-zero effort per deal, skip it.

principles.text: Influencer marketing sells borrowed trust; big creators and celebrities dilute it, so paying for reach alone rarely converts.
principles.quote: The entire product in influencer marketing is borrowed trust, and a celebrity post has none in it.

sources.title: Funnel congruency: why every step from ad to paywall must tell one story
sources.originalTitle: The Funnel Mechanics Masterclass
sources.summary: Jake Castillo argues that a frictionless app funnel depends on congruent messaging from top-of-funnel content through store page, onboarding and paywall. He borrows the native-ad funnel model, explains why one killer feature simplifies angles, and gives three benchmarks that diagnose which funnel step is broken.

principles.text: Make the funnel frictionless: customers should slide effortlessly down to the paywall, which requires every step to be congruent.
principles.quote: Your funnel needs to be as frictionless as possible.

principles.text: Carry the same language and pain point from top-of-funnel content through store page, onboarding and paywall.
principles.quote: Then every stage of the funnel afterwards (whether that’s your app store page or web2app funnel pages) need to carry the same messaging all the way through your onboarding to the paywall.

principles.text: Focus on one killer feature rather than several mediocre ones; it simplifies the marketing angles you use.
principles.quote: This is another reason why we only focused on one killer feature for Cal AI, and not 5 different mediocre ones, because this simplifies your marketing angles used to promote your product.

principles.text: Give prospects one idea to hold onto; each screen should confirm, not contradict, the story they're building.
principles.quote: Every screen after that either confirms or contradicts the story this prospect is constructing in their head about your solution.

principles.text: Native ad funnels work by educating first, so the product arrives as the answer to a problem, not a cold pitch.
principles.quote: And by then it doesn't feel like a pitch, it feels like the answer to a problem you are likely dealing with.

principles.text: Use benchmarks to locate the broken step: under 5 downloads/1,000 views, under 75% paywall rate, under 10% paywall conversion.
principles.quote: Under 5 downloads per 1,000 views? Your creative and your store page disagree.

sources.title: Mercenary vs missionary: match what you build to your core motivation
sources.originalTitle: Are You A Mercenary or Missionary??
sources.summary: Jake Castillo explains why six years of "discipline problems" in consulting were really a motivation mismatch. He splits operators into mercenaries (money-driven) and missionaries (need to care about the thing) and gives seven questions to ask before committing to a project, so you don't burn two years operating as the wrong type.

principles.text: Ask the identity question (mercenary or missionary) before the market question when choosing what to build.
principles.quote: But you should ask the identity question first, because it determines whether you'll still be putting in the necessary hours at fourteen months in.

principles.text: Mercenaries can grind boring, high-margin businesses for years; you don't need passion for the product.
principles.quote: If you're a mercenary, go find the boring high-margin thing and grind it out.

principles.text: Missionaries can't sustain effort on something they find pointless, even if the margins are great.
principles.quote: Put a missionary on a boring product with great margins and they'll quit in month four, and they won't be able to explain why, and they'll feel like a flake about it.

principles.text: Lack of focus is often a motivation mismatch, not a discipline problem.
principles.quote: The thing that six years of performance reviews couldn't fix, that no amount of discipline touched, evaporated the moment the work was mine and mattered to me.

principles.text: Test commitment by picturing the boring middle of the business and doing it daily for a year.
principles.quote: What's the boring middle of this business? Every business has one. Support tickets, ad reviews, contracts, reconciliation.

principles.text: Don't pick as one type and operate as the other; that's how you burn two years.

sources.title: How Jake Castillo diagnoses app growth with 4 metrics, learned scaling Cal AI to $50M ARR
sources.originalTitle: The ONLY 4 app metrics you should care about
sources.summary: Jake argues founders who say their app isn't growing usually can't name four core numbers: content/ad views, App Store impressions, paywall rate, and paywall conversion. Each metric points to a specific lever (traffic, message, or product), so you fix the furthest-off one instead of guessing. He shares Cal AI's benchmark targets.

principles.text: Track four numbers: views from content/ads, App Store impressions, paywall rate, and paywall conversion rate.
principles.quote: I usually stop them and ask if they know these 4 metrics:

principles.text: Cal AI's benchmarks: 5 downloads per 1,000 views, 75%+ paywall rate, 10% paywall conversion. Hit these and acquisition isn't the problem.
principles.quote: Hit those three consistently and you will not have a user acquisition problem.

principles.text: Judge influencer deals only on views turning into downloads and downloads turning into paying users, not followers, likes, or video polish.
principles.quote: Follower counts, likes, and how good the video looked never made the list.

principles.text: Low views means a traffic problem: post more, sign more creators, or run ads if you have capital.
principles.quote: If views are low, you have a traffic problem.

principles.text: High views but weak downloads means a message or demand problem: the hook is wrong or nobody wants the offer.
principles.quote: If views are high but downloads are weak, you have a message problem (or a demand problem).

principles.text: Strong downloads but weak conversion is a product problem. Fix whichever metric is furthest off first; everything else waits.
principles.quote: Whichever one is furthest off is your job for the next month.

sources.title: Beat your competitors in 30 days by protecting critical thinking and doing a month of deliberate practice
sources.originalTitle: How to beat 99% of your competitors in 30 days
sources.summary: Jake argues that AI makes people lazier and less able to think, so the way to beat competitors is to protect your own critical thinking. He recommends a 30-day, one-hour-a-day deliberate practice sprint on a skill you fear or are bad at, drawing on The First 20 Hours and Michael Smoak's 30-day video challenge.

principles.text: Practice and protect your ability to think critically; it is your edge as everyone else offloads thinking to AI.
principles.quote: you need to practice and protect your ability to think critically at all costs.

principles.text: Original thinking you can articulate clearly may be the most important skill to master going forward.
principles.quote: Harnessing the ability to think and have original thoughts that you can articulate intelligently might be the most important skill to master going forward.

principles.text: Heavy AI use can feel productive while wasting time on tasks you could do faster yourself.
principles.quote: sometimes I just waste time prompting AI to do something I could have cranked out in 20 mins myself

principles.text: You don't need 10,000 hours; one month of intense, real learning can set you apart from people who outsource thinking.
principles.quote: you could lock in for one month of real intense learning and catapult yourself into a whole new realm of possibilities.

principles.text: Lean into what you fear or dread; do the task you avoid, even if you'll be bad at it at first.
principles.quote: You’re going to suck at it at first, but that’s the point.

principles.text: Run a 30-day sprint: an hour a day on the skill that stresses you, without offloading your thinking to AI.
principles.quote: Lock yourself in a room for an hour everyday for a month and DO THE WORK

sources.title: Retention beyond the paywall: the 2:1 lifecycle email strategy for apps
sources.originalTitle: The Most UNDERRATED Retention Lever For Apps
sources.summary: Jake argues app founders stop marketing the moment someone downloads, leaving users with only billing emails. He recommends fixing the product first, then running a simple 2:1 email cadence (two value emails, one offer) plus a winback system for lapsed users.

principles.text: Use 15% annual retention as the working benchmark for consumer apps, so plan for churn and non-renewal.
principles.quote: For consumer apps, a 15% annual retention should be your working benchmark.

principles.text: Most apps have no system for winning back or keeping customers, then overspend on acquisition just to hold MRR flat.
principles.quote: But after consulting on over 100 apps, most have no system for winning back customers or preventing them from leaving in the first place.

principles.text: Email can't save a weak product. Find what retained users repeat and make that feature faster and more valuable.
principles.quote: Look at the behaviors retained users repeat, find the feature they use most, then make that experience faster, easier and more valuable.

principles.text: Start lifecycle email with a 2:1 ratio: two value emails for every one offer-based email.
principles.quote: a 2:1 ratio strategy is what I usually recommend to start with: Two emails that add value, One email that is offer based

principles.text: Monetization doesn't end at the first paywall. Existing users who understand the product are the best audience for the next relevant offer or upsell.
principles.quote: a customer who already understands your product is often the most logical person to show the next useful offer.

principles.text: Lapsed users often didn't hate the product, so a useful email lets you re-enter the conversation without re-buying their attention.
principles.quote: A useful email gives you a chance to re-enter the conversation without buying that person's attention all over again.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo, Cal AI's CMO and COO, explains how Cal AI reached 15M users and $40M ARR in 18 months. He covers niching down, choosing between UGC, influencers and paid ads by cash position, running about 300 paywall tests, pricing, LTV, and hiring hungry people.

chunks.heading: Cal AI go-to-market: how Jake got to 15M users and $40M ARR
chunks.text:
- Jake joined Cal AI as CMO and COO two days after quitting his consulting job.
- Cal AI launched in May 2024 and was acquired in December 2025, 18 months later.
- By then it had 15 million users, 300+ influencer and creator partnerships, and $40M ARR.
- Jake's first role was scaling the influencer program. He spent his days on calls with influencers, reviewing posts, and building systems to manage, track and attribute revenue across 300 of them.
- The pitch was a calorie tracker where you "just take a picture" of your food and the app calculates calories and macros.
- Jake's view of the old way: tracking by typing everything in "turns tracking your food into homework."
- On the 18-month run, he said the team "outworked everyone in the space."

chunks.heading: Saturation, differentiation, and niching down
chunks.text:
- Jake disagrees that saturation is a problem. A crowded market means people are actively engaged in that niche. If your product is better, the opportunity is there.
- Cal AI's edge was removing friction. The car-vs-horse-and-buggy analogy was his: people switch once they see the easier mode.
- Don't build a clone. Unless you improve on incumbents, you can grab some share with competent marketing but never reach something great.
- Look for industries that feel stagnant and haven't changed in about 5 years.
- Any feature can be made sexy with a unique spin. Calorie tracking wasn't seen as fun before Cal AI; they made it fun.
- His niche example is a workout tracker for new moms:
  - Pick a very specific avatar, since there are too many generalists and not enough "super targeted painpoint problem solvers."
  - Niche first, then marketing angle, then UI.
  - The niche tells you your ICP, what influencers and UGC creators should look like, and what paid ads should look like.
  - Make the UI look like the apps that audience already uses, so the app isn't intimidating.
- He would avoid social apps because of the cold start problem: you need a network effect to get a network effect.

chunks.heading: UGC strategy for apps
chunks.text:
- UGC is where Jake would start if launching an app today. Influencer prices have risen, while UGC creator prices have not really increased.
- The game is a swing at the algorithm. About 90% of UGC videos break even or lose money; the 10% that go viral make the money.
- Deal structure:
  - Start with low-risk, trial-based deals and no big upfront commitments.
  - Pay flat fees, not pay-per-view. Pay-per-view means you pay for all the views but give up the upside of a viral video.
  - His line: "Don't pay for viral hits."
  - Going viral is "not an if, it's a when" if you take enough shots on goal.
- Pick one of three formats (talking head, wall-of-text, skit) and only sign creators with a proven viral record in that exact format.
- Jake prefers going "deep and narrow" over "far and wide." Competitors get bored and chase shiny objects, so staying focused is where the success comes from.
- Without discipline it can be a money pit. He warns it's possible to spend $10K on UGC and end up at a $100 CPM.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing: when it works and how to pick creators
chunks.text:
- Influencers vs UGC creators:
  - With an influencer you pay for the trust they have with their existing audience.
  - With a UGC creator you pay for a swing at the algorithm on a new account dedicated to your brand.
- Check three things before choosing influencers:
  1. There are a lot of creators in your niche.
  2. You aren't competing with brands whose LTV and average order value let them outbid you. Example: a fashion brand with ~$1,000 LTV vs an app with $10/month and ~$30 LTV.
  3. The creators have high-value audiences.
- Cal AI's situation fit this:
  - Health and fitness had millions of creators.
  - Most weren't monetizing through brand deals, because few brands were available (protein powders, a few fitness fashion brands) and many paid only commission.
  - Creators were desperate for deals, so Cal AI signed hundreds at favorable CPMs.
  - Their audiences were cult-like ("I want to look just like you").
- Jake's creator-quality test is the comment section, a lesson from co-founder Blake Anderson:
  - Look for whether the creator connects with their audience and has real conversations.
  - Back-end revenue numbers shared by agencies or creators can't be trusted.
  - "You can't fake the comment section."

chunks.heading: Paid ads and choosing a channel by stage
chunks.text:
- Early on, Cal AI ran influencer videos as paid ads in Meta, with decent results.
- Jake says they misunderstood what you pay for in paid ads:
  - UGC: a swing at the algorithm.
  - Influencers: audience trust.
  - Paid ads: clicks, one to one, with no algorithmic lift from virality.
- So paid ad creative should be hard-selling. UGC and influencer content has to hide the ad so viewers don't swipe; paid ads don't.
- Cal AI found success with paid ads once they made dedicated paid ad creative instead of reusing seamless organic influencer videos.
- Paid ads should have the highest view-to-subscription conversion, since the click goes straight to the app store. If they don't, "we got to look at your paid ads."
- Highest converting is not the same as most profitable. A $100 UGC video with 10M views can beat $100 in Meta on cash-on-cash return even with a poor conversion rate.
- Jake's stage framework:
  - No money: UGC. Everyone has a phone and can create the content themselves.
  - Some budget: influencers.
  - Cash flow isn't a concern and you're scaling: paid ads. Done right it's a "money printing machine" (a dollar in, two out). It isn't the most profitable but it is the most scalable.
- He notes the pattern: beginners say paid ads, the middle plays influencers and UGC, and the people making hundreds of millions per year say paid ads are the only place to play.
- On AI UGC and AI influencers, he says it doesn't matter: "good marketing material is good marketing material," and a cheap 50-cent CPM on bad content still converts at zero. AI UGC wasn't good enough while Cal AI was scaling, so they didn't use it.

chunks.heading: Pricing and paywall testing
chunks.text:
- Cal AI priced below every competitor on purpose. The calorie tracking TAM was huge, and the aim was to gain mindshare by being the cheaper alternative.
- The target audience was young and chronically online, with less disposable income. Cheaper pricing also made it easy to convert users of other apps.
- Pricing depends on TAM:
  - A broad, general-population app that "talks to everyone" should price lower so price is never the deciding factor.
  - A smaller, targeted app (like the new-moms workout planner) can charge more, because the TAM is small and the avatar thinks "this is for me."
- Tactical rule of thumb:
  - Benchmark competitors, then start 20% cheaper.
  - Go 20% higher to be the prestige option.
  - Match their prices for bar-for-bar.
  - Then keep testing.
- Testing cadence at Cal AI:
  - About four paywall tests a week, roughly 300 tests over 18 months.
  - Having fewer than one or two live tests at a time meant they were "dropping the ball."
  - Individual tests were estimated to add $50,000, $20,000 or $10,000 in monthly revenue.
  - Each test took about 20 to 30 minutes to launch.
- Start testing once you get about 100 users a day.
- Why LTV matters most: "the way apps win is who can spend the most to acquire a customer," and LTV determines that. "The only way you will be able to durably win is if you can acquire customers at a higher cost than your competitors."

chunks.heading: AI in apps, hiring, and co-founders
chunks.text:
- Most "AI" apps add little value. Jake sees real value now in agentic use cases, where AI does the work.
  - Example: co-founder Henry Langmack's app Soore books flights end to end, including seat preference, passport info, check-in, and rebooking.
  - His filter: if your mom knows about the tool, it's popular enough that you have to provide real value, with no misinformation arbitrage left.
- Co-founders:
  - Align on the mission first (pump and dump, sell, or change the world). Misalignment is "a recipe for disaster."
  - Pick complementary skills (technical plus creative), not similar ones.
  - He joined Cal AI to be near Zach Yadegari, "the smartest person I've ever met."
- Hiring at Cal AI:
  - For hard-to-teach skills (e.g. AI systems), hire experienced people.
  - For easy-to-teach skills (e.g. marketing, which is mostly basic principles), hire for "hunger and drive and work ethic."
  - Every marketer Cal AI hired had no prior experience. Jake wanted a blank canvas with no bad habits to unlearn.
  - He preferred people without other opportunities: "who's the least picky eater in the world? Someone that's been starving."
- His closing advice: it's "not that hard" if you take the bet on yourself, execute every day, and outwork the competition.
- When he left his job, his goal was $10K a month; at points Cal AI did that in an hour.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo, Cal AI co-founder, explains how the team scaled via fitness creators: picking niches whose audiences actually want the product, structuring deals around RPM, and layering paid ads on top. He covers the magic moment test, reading comments instead of views, low-price strategy, and doing unglamorous outreach for 18 months.

chunks.heading: Choosing creators and niches: the "magic moment" and creator-app fit
chunks.text:
- Jake's thesis for Cal AI: a calorie tracker is used most by people into health and fitness. That niche has more creators than any other, but few brands to work with (protein powder, athleisure), so many creators had never had a brand deal.
- Creators already made "what I eat in a day" videos, about one a week, so Cal AI slotted in by scanning the food on camera.
- Dawson proved the format converted. The team then copied and pasted it across the many fitness creators making the same content.
- He says the playbook only works if those conditions hold for your app. Example: an astrology app has no millions of creators, and the few brands in that space have likely signed exclusivity deals.
- Cal AI had a "magic moment": a one-two-three punch of scan, analyze, results. Viewers did a double take ("Whoa, what was it?").
- Without a magic moment, an integration gets blinked past and won't convert. In that case he says paid ads with a hard sell fit better.
- The magic moment must be digestible in seconds and need no long explanation. Otherwise it feels like an ad, won't go viral and won't be profitable.

chunks.heading: Small product details that made creator content work
chunks.text:
- The team built a creator-specific build of the app. The scan screen showed the Cal AI name and logo so the marketing message was clear.
- Cal AI has a streaks feature. The streak popup appeared after a scan and interrupted the three-step sequence, so creators were told not to show their first scan of the day.
- Jake notes people digest things in threes, and the streak added an unwanted fourth beat.
- With subtle integrations, they added an on-screen caption "tracked with Cal AI". With less subtle ones, they dropped the caption because it hurt views.
- His rule: "no marketing program should ever feel like a finished product." Keep testing and adapting.

chunks.heading: Building creator relationships and why copycats failed
chunks.text:
- Dawson was one of the first creators contacted. Jake says he did anything asked, iterated on formats and angles, and never nickel-and-dimed. The team gave him bonuses and he became a close friend.
- Jake's advice: early on you have few creators, so there is no excuse not to build personal relationships. A creator who loves working with you refers friends and shouts about you; a miserable brand gets no referrals.
- If you treat it as strictly transactional, it stays transactional.
- The team built publicly on Twitter and shared wins and failures, which drew many clones. Jake wasn't worried: the clones weren't obsessed the way he was. He says he dreamed about signing influencers.
- Small incremental improvements compound into a mountain competitors can't climb.
- Clone coverage sent traffic to Cal AI: Twitter threads about clones' revenue, and searches for "AI calorie tracker" that surfaced Cal AI first in Google and the App Store.
- Hard work and dedication increase your "surface area for luck."

chunks.heading: Reading comments to qualify niches and creators
chunks.text:
- Quote: "views can lie, followers can lie, but comments cannot. The truth is always in the comments."
- Niche test: read the comments on big creators in that space. If people are looking for a solution your app provides, go full steam ahead.
- Creator test: for roughly every 10 creators, nine won't convert and one will. Comments tell you which.
- Bad sign: a comment section of fire emojis and sweating-face emojis (for example, under a female creator's leg-day video).
- Good sign: comments like "thank you for posting this, I didn't know how to work my hamstrings/quads/glutes."
- You want a cult-like following, not just a following. It is a lagging indicator. Great creators will get one, so look for diamonds in the rough with good content and low views, and sign them cheaper.
- Example: a creator who was about the 12th to 15th Jake signed was getting 10-12k views. In month three one video hit 7 million, and he never fell below 500k after. Jake connected him with other brands.

chunks.heading: Niches that failed and what he learned
chunks.text:
- UFC creators: the thesis was that fighters track calories to cut weight. Several big creators were signed, with thousands of dollars spent each, and posted to crickets, with no download spike.
- Why it failed: the typical UFC viewer is on a couch with beer and pizza. They want to watch someone else do a restrictive diet, not track their own.
- Mukbang creators: eating 10-20k calories on camera looked like a big wow factor. It also failed because viewers see it as a reward or cheat day and don't want calorie information.
- Lesson: understand not just what content a creator makes but why viewers consume it and their psychological motivations.
- Big bold bets were a core value. For every deal that loses a couple thousand dollars, one wins hundreds of thousands. After a failure, dig into why it failed instead of skipping it.

chunks.heading: Pricing creators: RPM cap, flat rates and bonuses
chunks.text:
- The real money in influencer and UGC marketing is in viral hits. Set your break-even on a creator's average views, and the occasional mega-viral video is profit.
- Flat-rate deals capture that asymmetric upside, so use them whenever possible. Jake also used bonuses and scaled deals.
- Step 1: know your revenue per thousand views (RPM) in the niche. You cannot pay a CPM above that RPM or you are guaranteed to lose money ("it's just math"). Some creators will say no, and that is fine.
- Step 2: estimate the creator's expected views and set a profitable CPM-based rate on that.
- When a creator asks for something like $1,000 a month, meeting their cash demand often lets you raise the deliverables.
- Be human, not a "sleazy agent." If it doesn't work, decline kindly and refer them to a friend who fits.
- Early on, RPM is easy to see: no posts means no downloads, so a post shows as a spike (for example, creator X got 1,000 views and $Y revenue). Jake wasn't sure of the exact figure and says it's either a $10 or $1 RPM, so treat that number as unconfirmed.
- At scale, attribution is murky. When 50 to 70 influencers post per day, you analyze secondary metrics (comments, likes, saves) and incrementality tests, such as looking at the demographics of a creator's following and where the spike appears.
- Jake created a "renewal score" at Cal AI that combined many metrics to decide whether to renew a creator.
- He gave bonuses even when not required ("dude you crushed it this month"). He says nobody does that and it pays off over time.

chunks.heading: Sourcing and managing creators at scale
chunks.text:
- The secret is working really hard for a really long time. The team sent thousands of messages for 18 months, most went unanswered, many replies demanded rates they couldn't afford, and every negotiation was "pulling teeth."
- It never stopped being a grind: "we weren't stopping until we were the number one calorie tracker in the world."
- In 2026 creators are savvier, charge higher rates and have negotiation courses. Demand rose while supply stayed flat. Jake says it is harder but also easier, with tools like Codex and Claude Code. If it's hard to sign creators, your competitors won't do it.
- Management consulting taught him systems. Early on he ran everything in Google Sheets (his "magnum office"), later built formal software.
- That software, Rally, is built for influencer and UGC marketing. It stores deals, automates contract sending, auto-tracks posts and views, computes view bonuses and payment amounts, and gives a renewal score. He planned to launch around the end of October 2026.
- He also does consulting; people can reach him via Twitter and LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: Paid ads, funnel congruency and pricing
chunks.text:
- Jake says paid ads are easier than influencers: creative can be bought, and tools like Tribe let you get creative for free and pay a percentage of ad spend (aligned incentives). Influencers have friction in outreach, negotiation, management and murky attribution.
- Cal AI began spending on paid roughly a couple of months in, and paid grew as a share of the marketing mix. He says to diversify risk.
- At first they recycled influencer content. Later they invested in dedicated paid creative, which performed far better.
- Why: organic content swings for a viral home run with a subtle integration. In paid you pay for every view, so make every view understand the product with a hard sell. The hook must relate to the product (for example, a baseball hook for a pitching app, not an accounting app).
- He learned a lot from the Speechify team on paid creative.
- Keep the ad, onboarding and app experience congruent, like a hotel lobby that matches its rooms. In onboarding, hit the pain points from the marketing, drive home the impact of the pain, then present the solution.
- Pricing: Cal AI is about $30 a year. Co-founder Blake Anderson insisted they optimize for mindshare, not profit. The audience is young with little disposable income and hasn't suffered the problem as long, so it hurts less and they pay less.
- Jake's warning: copying what Cal AI did (or something from a podcast) is the easiest way to burn money, because your app isn't ours. Think about your market, pain point and motivation.
- Affiliates: anyone could sign up in the app and earn $10 per sale (not per download), a one-time payment, about 33% on gross.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo explains how Cal AI grew by signing hundreds of health and fitness creators who scan food on camera. He covers creator selection by views, CPM versus RPM math, capped view bonuses, UGC economics, and constant testing.

chunks.heading: How Cal AI found its influencer marketing playbook and the niche it ran on
chunks.text:
- Jake credits co-founder Blake Anderson with the original playbook. Blake had scaled his app UMAX with influencer marketing, and Cal AI ran the same principles: "let's test this out with this influencer marketing strategy."
- Jake says it "just took off like we couldn't have imagined." The team's job was then to take the ball and scale it as high as possible.
- Jake picked the health and fitness niche because it is oversaturated with creators and short on brands. There are only so many protein powder and athleisure companies, so many creators made content but had no way to monetize.
- Cal AI offered those creators a brand deal. The content integration was seamless because they already post "what I eat in a day" and weight loss or muscle building videos that show their food. The ask was to scan the food with Cal AI before eating it on camera.
- Creators said yes because it was easy, did not interrupt their content schedule, and was the first time they could monetize their work.
- After signing creators, the next problem was managing 300+ influencers at once.

chunks.heading: Influencer vs UGC creators: how to work with each
chunks.text:
- **Influencer:** an established creator with an existing audience and trust. They will not make every video about you. Maybe one or two videos a month. You are paying for the audience and trust they built.
- **UGC creator:** a regular person who makes a brand new account dedicated to your product (for example "Jake eats" with every video about Cali). They have around 10 followers, and videos only spread if the algorithm picks them up.
- **Influencers:** do not micromanage. "They're the artists. Let them paint." Give general integration guidelines only (how the app is shown, how many seconds in it appears, a caption tag), then "let them cook."
  - Cal AI gave full creative control. Influencers called it the easiest brand deal they ever had.
  - The common mistake is forcing an influencer into an infomercial-style script. The video then gets 50,000 views instead of the 1 million the CPM was priced on, and the brand is thousands of dollars in the red.
  - Have creators make their normal content and slide the app into it. That lets you estimate average views with confidence.
- **UGC creators:** micromanage them, since they have no audience. Steal viral formats that have already been proven.
- Jake sources UGC creators by searching "UGC creator" on the explore page and picking ones who feel like real people, not "NPC bots reading a script."
  - Sideshift has millions of creators and lets you post a job, but he thinks 99% of applicants are not good creators.
  - A brand new UGC account tends to be shown in the country the creator posts from. Influencers matter by where their audience is, not where they live, so ask for audience demographics.

chunks.heading: Testing mindset and risk tolerance
chunks.text:
- Jake's motto is "ABT: always be testing." He says if you are not testing new things "you're leaving money on the table."
- Example: Cal AI tested moving the app integration earlier and earlier in the video to find the earliest point that did not hurt views. For Cal AI that landed in roughly the 20-30 second range.
- He warns against copying numbers bar for bar. A friend's app has its sweet spot at the 60-second mark, and copying Cal AI's timing would have cut his views. "What works for my app may not work for your app." Take the principle and test the specifics.
- Cal AI's co-founders were 17, 18 and 23, and Jake was the oldest with a mortgage and a girlfriend (now wife). He says the team's risk tolerance was far higher than his, and he held on to his seat during the crazy tests.
- His lesson: have an incredibly high risk tolerance, because big bets give the asymmetric payout, and "otherwise you're just never going to learn."
- Cal AI kept exploring new creator niches. Mukbang creators and UFC fighters did not work. New moms did.
- A winning format "exists on a spectrum." The first video showed signs of life and Cal AI kept optimizing. "Cali is not a finished product. Our marketing system is not done and it never will be."

chunks.heading: Pricing creators: RPM vs CPM, view bonuses and caps
chunks.text:
- **Core rule:** the CPM only needs to be lower than your RPM (revenue per thousand views). Do not chase a fixed CPM. Measure how much revenue each thousand views produces, and keep your CPM under it.
- Competing for the same creators gets harder when other brands have far higher RPMs. A clothing brand with a $200 average order and $1,000 lifetime value can afford much higher CPMs than an app with a $30 order and $50 lifetime value.
- **CPM ceiling by channel:**
  - Paid ads can afford the highest CPM because the ad links straight to the app (least friction, highest conversion).
  - Influencers need a lower CPM because the viewer must leave the app, search the App Store and download.
  - UGC needs the lowest CPM because it has the same friction plus no brand trust from a brand new account.
- **Influencer deals:** a base rate plus view bonuses. Example from the talk: "$400 for four posts," asking for cross-posting to both platforms casually ("it's all good, you're already making the video"). Jake says creators usually agree if you do not make it a big deal.
- Estimate views conservatively: look at the creator's last 20 videos and average the 5 worst. He prices on that worst-case average, since all deal videos are unlikely to be the worst ones and anything above is profit.
- **View bonuses:** cap them, usually around 1 million views.
  - Most UGC videos get 500 to 1,000 views and lose money. The profit comes from the one or two videos a month that go viral, and paying for every view eats that upside.
  - People do not feel the difference between 1 million and 2 million, though it is double.
  - Very viral videos reach a broad, untargeted audience that converts worse. His example is Pizza Rat: "the first 100,000 viewers might" subscribe, but the later hundred million views were not worth much.
- **UGC pay structure:** about $25-30 per video as a base (roughly $600 a month), plus a view bonus. Example from the talk: a creator with one 1M-view video would be around $2 CPM, or roughly $1,000 total for about 1.5M views (roughly $1.50 CPM).

chunks.heading: Choosing influencers: views over followers
chunks.text:
- Jake's contrarian take: "We don't care about followers." What matters is average views per video. A creator with 1M followers who gets 1,000 views speaks to only those 1,000 people.
- The best targets already get strong views but have few followers (for example averaging a million views with 500 followers). They are not used to big brand-deal rates, so a reasonable offer feels generous, while brands that pay by following give inflated rates.
- **View range:** his minimum is about 25,000 views per video, because an influencer with 10,000 views takes the same management effort as one with 1M views. He sees the sweet spot as roughly 25,000 to 1M views per video.
  - Creators getting millions of views have a more general, less loyal audience and are less likely to be trusted on recommendations.
  - Cult-like audiences convert best.
- **Comment sections signal conversion:** a comment section of "fire emoji, fire emoji" converts poorly. One with a real community converts far better (for example people thanking the creator and sharing their own struggles, with replies between commenters).
- **Detecting fake views and comments:** click the commenters' profiles. Bots have zero posts, follow about 10 people and have zero followers, and the same fake-looking accounts comment on every video. Jake says he has been burned this way himself.
- He treats TikTok and Instagram as roughly the same bucket. Some apps do about 1.2x better on one or the other, so "you're majoring in the minors" if you obsess over it.

chunks.heading: Download, paywall and conversion benchmarks
chunks.text:
- Benchmark for organic content: **3 to 7 downloads per 1,000 views**.
- Funnel targets he cites: at least 75% of downloaders reach the paywall, and at least 10% of those subscribe.
- Content style does not matter to him as long as it converts: "I don't care what the content's like. As long as it converts, it's cool with me." That includes faceless content.
- **Attribution:** it gets harder with scale.
  - Cal AI now has millions of videos, and old videos still produce views, which pollutes the data.
  - Early on, every influencer video produced a visible download spike. With a baseline of around 100 downloads an hour, a post would push it to about 200, and they could tie the spike to that creator.
  - Early on, learn what comment sections and content formats look like for converting creators, then extrapolate from that.
  - At scale, "you have to almost become a data analyst," using methods like incrementality tests.

chunks.heading: Scaling operations: outreach and creator management
chunks.text:
- Cal AI sent so many DMs that TikTok and Instagram blocked further messages for the day. The fix was creating about 20 additional Cal AI accounts, one per outreach specialist, each messaging hundreds of creators a day.
- Outreach tactics:
  - Put a name to the message so they know they are not talking to a faceless brand.
  - Send a voice memo instead of a wall of text. Record it once and reuse it across creators, so it feels personal but scales.
- Jake built an internal tool to manage creators at volume. One click sends a contract. After signing, the creator gets a text with the content brief and asks which day works. That day feeds a content calendar, and every morning the team gets a batch of texts to send to creators scheduled to post. He calls it his "magnum opus."

chunks.heading: When to add paid ads and how to find an app idea
chunks.text:
- Paid ads: add them as soon as cash flow allows. Influencers and UGC are volatile because they depend on views, while Meta spending $500 a day "will consistently get your ROAS."
- At the start Cal AI used influencer and UGC content as its ad creative because it had no budget for anything else. Now paid ads are a full department with dedicated paid-ad creators. Paid creatives are written differently from organic ones because you pay for every view with no algorithmic push. The product appears earlier and is a harder sell ("hey guys, let me tell you about Cali").
- If he started from scratch today, with a different financial situation, Jake would begin with paid ads. Eighteen months ago he would have started with UGC.
- He says he and the team were also running web-to-app campaigns, and sees an arbitrage between Eastern Europe (heavy on web-to-app) and the US (heavy on influencer/UGC).
- **Finding an app idea:**
  - Pick a niche you are genuinely interested in. He says he woke up excited to build Cal AI, which he doubts would be true for a period tracker.
  - Think about apps you use daily and how to make them better, then take an existing app and make it 10% better or 10% less friction.
- On copycats: copying a successful app leads to limited outcomes. Cal AI was not the first calorie tracker; it took the concept and made it more interesting and better. "You're never going to make the money that you're hoping for" by blatantly copying.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo, former CMO of Cal AI, lays out a five-step UGC creator system for taking an app from zero to $10K/month: source talking-head creators, warm up dedicated accounts, pick a content format (magic moment vs painful problem), run RPM vs CPM economics, then cut and scale creators. Includes concrete pricing, benchmarks and ratios.

chunks.heading: Zero to $10K/month with UGC creators: the overall playbook
chunks.text:
- Jake Castillo co-founded Cal AI and served as CMO. Cal AI launched in May 2024, scaled to 15 million users in under 18 months, and was acquired by MyFitnessPal.
- His core claim is that an app can go from zero to $10K a month using UGC alone, without raising money or spending heavily on paid ads.
- Cal AI's primary growth channel was influencer marketing, and a big part of his job was "figuring out how to turn creators into subscriptions."
- The five-step system is: find creators, warm up accounts, pick a content format, analyze economics, then cut and scale.
- His closing advice: "it's not easy, but it is simple." No genius, technical depth or funding is needed. What matters is doing the boring work repeatedly: source creators, test content, measure, cut what fails, double down on what works, and keep at it "longer and with more discipline than everyone else."

chunks.heading: Why UGC creators instead of big influencers, and how to find them
chunks.text:
- His principle: "good outputs start with great inputs, and creators are your inputs." The best scripts and app can't fix a delivery person who isn't compelling.
- Influencer marketing is more competitive because AI has increased the number of apps launched, so more companies chase the same influencers. Paying large influencers is expensive for a small startup or solo founder.
- A UGC creator is an everyday person who creates a brand new account dedicated to your product. What you pay for is reach.
- Where to find them:
  - Post a job on platforms like SideShift and get hundreds of applicants overnight.
  - Search "UGC creator" directly on TikTok and Instagram.
- Filter for talking-head content, because it converts better and feels more trustworthy.
- Signals of a good creator:
  - Natural camera presence, charisma and good energy.
  - Feels like they're FaceTiming a friend rather than reading a script.
  - At least one talking-head video with a million views ("they got the juice").
- Pricing structure:
  - Start with a small test: about 10 test videos at $10 each.
  - If the videos are good, move to a full campaign: 30 videos a month at $30 per video.
  - Add bonuses at view milestones such as 100k, 500k and 1 million views.
- UGC creators usually come to you, so respond quickly. For negotiating, he advises getting on a call as soon as possible, because "it is much easier to win a negotiation over a call than over email."

chunks.heading: Warming up creator accounts so they don't get shadowbanned
chunks.text:
- Have each creator make a brand new account dedicated specifically to your app.
- Warm-up routine:
  - About 30 minutes a day watching content in the niche they'll post in.
  - Liking videos, commenting and engaging like a normal user.
  - Publishing a few videos in the niche without mentioning your brand.
- Reason: TikTok and Instagram know UGC creators make branded content that amounts to free advertisement. If they identify an account as a creator account, they shadowban it, keep it out of the algorithm and prevent real views.
- Only once a video breaks 1,000 views should the creator begin posting branded content.
- The warm-up also works as a test of whether the creator is willing to follow your process.

chunks.heading: Choosing a content format: magic moment vs. painful problem
chunks.text:
- He calls content format "undoubtedly the most important part of the entire process" because it determines installs. He uses a simple decision tree.
- **Question 1: does the app have a magic moment?** This is a feature so visually impressive that viewers do a double take on seeing it on screen. Cal AI is his example.
  - If yes, maximize views. The creator makes the most viral story possible, finds a natural point to integrate the app, demonstrates the magic moment, and lets the product sell itself.
  - These videos get more views and a lower conversion rate. The extra reach should offset the lower conversion.
- **Question 2 (no magic moment): does the app solve a painful problem?**
  - If yes, maximize intent. Spend the start of the video making the problem feel real, so the viewer thinks "oh my god, like me," then introduce the app as the solution.
  - These videos get fewer views but convert much better.
  - If no, he would "seriously reconsider" the product or its positioning.
- He credits co-founder Blake Anderson with the idea of starting from the marketing angle first and building the product backwards from the viral content idea.
- On creative control: he lets creators cook within their domain of expertise. He gives general guidelines rather than dedicated scripts, because "I'm not a great creator, but I recognize that."

chunks.heading: Measuring whether creator content makes money: CPM, installs and RPM
chunks.text:
Jake's worked example:
- Pay $900 for 30 videos that get 600k views, which is a $1.50 CPM.
- At 2 installs per 1,000 views, 600k views yields 1.2k installs.
- At a 10% install-to-paid conversion rate ("pretty standard"), that is about 120 paying users.
- At a $20 average order value, that is $2.4k in revenue from $900 of spend.
- Revenue per 1,000 views (RPM) is $4. Paying a $1.50 CPM to earn a $4 RPM means "I'm ready to scale."

Realism check:
- 30 videos a month at $30 each is $900 of spend, which most creators will accept.
- Reaching 600k views usually needs only one or two low-level viral videos, not even a million-view video.
- Two installs per 1,000 views should be the bare minimum. Below that, there is a content problem or an app problem.
- UGC is "not for the faint of heart." Accounts have no following, so 20 videos might all land under 5K views before the 21st gets 200K.

chunks.heading: Reviewing creators: assume you'll cut everyone
chunks.text:
- He starts the analysis assuming he will cut every creator, then requires each creator's data to give a reason to renew them.
- Three things he checks:
  1. **Economics:** did the revenue from their views justify what was paid for those views?
  2. **Intent:** read the comment sections for people asking "what app is that?" or tagging friends ("you need to see this"). This shows real interest in the product.
  3. **Correlation:** cross-reference viral videos with App Store Connect data to see whether a spike in views matched a spike in downloads.
- These checks separate vanity metrics from real business results.
- Ideally, for every creator cut, bring in two replacements.
- He frames this as a different hat from building: growth economics and analysis, with constant testing of creators and content types.

chunks.heading: Scaling the creator program and what revenue to expect
chunks.text:
- Scaling path: from 5 creators to 100, 200 and 300.
- At 5 to 10 creators you can manage it yourself. Around 50 active creators, hire a dedicated creator manager, at roughly one manager per 50 active creators.
- By that point the content format and frameworks are in place, and the hard part is organization. Many tools exist for managing creators, and he says to find a system that works for you and double down on it.
- Rough revenue by program size:
  - 5 to 10 creators: about $10K a month.
  - About 50 creators: roughly $100K to $200K a month.
  - 100 to 300 creators: can reach the millions.
- Returns scale asymmetrically "because that's how virality works."
- He shares more tactical detail in his newsletter, covering topics like onboarding, creating a good viral video, signing a first creator and reviewing creators.

chunks.heading: Summary
