chunks.text: Jake Castillo, Cal AI co-founder, explains the bootstrapped influencer-marketing playbook behind Cal AI's growth to $50M ARR and the My Fitness Pal exit. He covers replicating winning creator formats, vetting creators in seconds, writing outreach DMs, paying upfront, and the work ethic required.

chunks.heading: Getting from $9.50 in the bank to a $50M ARR exit: the founding path
chunks.text:
- Jake was a management consultant who hated the job, riding a two-hour train each way and watching YouTube.
- A video of Oliver Brcado explaining how Tabs chocolate went from zero to millions a month online showed him a path he hadn't known existed. He followed Oliver on Twitter for weeks, unsure it was real.
- When Oliver tweeted that he needed a head of operations for Study Buddy, Jake DM'd him offering to fix operations for free. His pitch: "All we do is go into businesses to streamline their operations." Oliver replied within an hour.
- He moonlighted on Study Buddy after work. There he met Zach Yadegari, who was 16 and shadowing Oliver. Jake spent time making sure Zach actually learned things (paid ads, org structure).
- Jake quit his corporate job and left Study Buddy. Two days later Zach called about an app he'd been building and asked Jake to run operations and scaling. That became Cal AI.
- Cal AI was fully bootstrapped and reinvested everything for over a year before the founders took out any money.
- Jake had a mortgage, student loans and a fiancée. He burned his savings, pulled from his 401k, borrowed from his girlfriend, and fought daily to avoid overdrafts.
- Cal AI went from early stage to $50M a year in recurring revenue and an exit to MyFitnessPal in about 18 months, with no outside funding.
- Jake's framing: as revenue rose he felt like the poorest he'd ever been, because nothing came out of the business.

chunks.heading: The core growth engine: influencer "what I eat in a day" integrations
chunks.text:
- The first test was a fitness influencer posting a "what I eat in a day" video and scanning each meal with Cal AI. Downloads spiked instantly, bigger than anything they had seen.
- His consulting-derived rule: "when you see something that works, don't try and reinvent the wheel. Just try and replicate and do it over and over until it stops working."
- They signed as many fitness influencers as possible and asked for the same format. Every video crushed it.
- One team kept signing new fitness creators. Another explored new niches (teenage girls, new moms) to see whether the same format would replicate.
- Once a formula works in a niche, find as many influencers as possible in it and have them copy and paste it.
- Jake's view: the hard work is sustained volume of this loop, not a secret formula.

chunks.heading: Fitting the product into each creator's existing content
chunks.text:
- When expanding to new niches, Jake does not make creators change their format. He asks how the app can fit into their normal content.
- The reason is economics. Sponsored posts that deviate from a creator's usual style tend to be their worst performers.
- Profitability is calculated off CPM based on the creator's average views. The goal is to make the floor of a sponsored video their average views, with the ceiling being an outlier hit.
- Example: if a TikTok dancer has never done "what I eat in a day," forcing that format risks a video that badly underperforms.
- Seamless vs hard sell depends on two questions about the product:
  - Is it easy to understand?
  - Does it have a magic moment?
- If yes to both, do a seamless integration. Viewers think "wait, what was that?" and understand it immediately.
- Cal AI fit this: everyone knows calorie tracking, and snapping a photo to get calories was jaw-dropping in early 2024.
- If the product is harder to understand or has no wow moment, use a more explicit hard sell.

chunks.heading: Picking niches: supply, demand and price
chunks.text:
- Fitness had many creators relative to advertiser demand, which gave favorable pricing versus mass UGC or paid ads.
- Niches where supply is thin and demand is high are expensive or locked up by exclusivity deals.
- Fashion is a bad fit for apps: brands there have an order value in the hundreds of dollars (up to about $200) and can pay high CPMs, while an app's order value is about $30 to $50. Skincare and other consumer packaged goods have the same problem.
- Jake's under-used opportunity: college kids.
  - There are many of them and few brands know how to work with them.
  - They need some money but not much, and have time to spare, so they accept lower CPMs than white-collar professionals.
  - He says he doesn't see many apps using them successfully.

chunks.heading: Vetting influencers in 10 to 20 seconds
chunks.text:
Jake reviewed over 10,000 influencer profiles and worked with roughly 300 for Cal AI. His checklist:

- **Views:** at least about 25,000 plus views per video. Managing a 20,000-view creator takes the same effort as a 1M-view creator (messaging, scheduling, reviewing posts, comments, renewals, payment), so spend bandwidth on bigger fish.
- **Comment quality:** he wants real comments like "thank you for posting this workout, I had no idea what to do in the gym, you're a lifesaver," not strings of fire or flexing emojis.
- **Replies within comment threads:** people replying to each other, even disagreeing, show a real community. "True communities convert better than anything else."
- **Parasocial connection:** does the creator talk to the audience (talking head, voiceover, personality) or just show their body. Talking creators build the relationship that leads to conversions.
- Final gut test he cites: does this person look like someone you'd want to be friends with.
- Three videos of scrolling is usually enough.

chunks.heading: Writing outreach DMs creators actually open
chunks.text:
- Start from first principles: put yourself in the creator's shoes. They get 100+ DMs a day, so most outreach is ignored.
- The message preview is what gets opened. Lead with "paid promo" and that you want to pay them.
- Skip the life story, the bootstrapped-founder pitch or telling them you're a fan. "Everyone is selfishly motivated."
- Keep it short: paid promo, want to make a video for me, I'll pay X. The goal is an easy yes or no, or the start of a negotiation.
- Whether to state a dollar figure depends on the creator:
  - A college kid new to paid promos: mention a figure, since even $100 impresses.
  - A wealthy, experienced creator such as a stay-at-home mom with many brand deals: don't open with a number. Say "I want to do a paid promo with you, what would you be looking for?" and let her start the money conversation.
- Pay upfront and say so. Creators have been burned by sketchy brands, so this removes their risk and shows you have the money, which matters since Jake looks young.
- Same principle applies in reverse for pitching him: he turns down "take you out for coffee" invites because an hour for a $5 coffee isn't worth his bandwidth, and he responds to concrete value (for example, proof of prior reach).

chunks.heading: Operating cadence and the volume behind the results
chunks.text:
- Jake rejects the idea that copycats are a threat. He says nobody else will do the volume and the hours, and that whoever works hardest wins.
- His routine during Cal AI's growth:
  - Up around 6 a.m. Pacific to overlap with co-founders on Eastern time.
  - Reviewed prior-day posts and overnight submissions from international influencers, gave feedback.
  - Calls with influencers all day, fixing tracking sheets and sending contracts between calls.
  - Also handled accounting, legal and meetings with his co-founders.
  - From about 6 p.m. to midnight Pacific, when co-founders were asleep, was his deep-work block.
  - Often fell asleep with the laptop on his lap, and sometimes did not leave the house from Monday to Thursday.
  - Roughly two years of 20-hour days.
- Speed mattered: if an influencer replied and had five minutes to talk, he jumped on a call immediately, including middle-of-the-night calls with creators in Eastern Europe.
- On hunger: "Anyone can work for 20 hours a day for one day." What separates great from average is doing it with no end in sight.
- His test for yourself: if you are asking whether you are working hard enough, you are not.

chunks.heading: Advice for people thinking of leaving a job to build apps
chunks.text:
- Corporate jobs aren't safe, since someone else signs your paycheck. "The safest bet is the bet you take on yourself."
- There are people earning 10x more who are 10x less capable, so go do it.
- The path is simple but not easy: find an idea you like, build it so it works, and get it in front of people for less than it costs them to buy.
- Specifically: acquire customers at a cost lower than what they pay. If you do that, "you're going to be fine."
- There is no secret hack. "The secret hack is working your ass off for an unbelievably long time."
- He advises surrounding yourself with exceptional people. His three co-founders are his biggest inspirations: Blake Anderson for creative ideation, Zach Yadegari for logical first-principles thinking, and Henry for technical ability.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo, who ran marketing and operations at Cal AI from zero to $50M ARR in about 18 months, lists 34 operator lessons. Themes: diagnose the funnel constraint before adding traffic, price creators on total cost and variance, keep features and retention loops tied to core value, and treat execution volume as the real moat.

chunks.heading: Diagnosing the funnel before scaling
chunks.text:
- Jake's frame from scaling Cal AI to $50M ARR in roughly 18 months (he ran marketing and day-to-day operations): "You CANNOT scale a broken machine." Founders ask "How do I get more users?" when the real question is where the machine is broken.
- His diagnostic map:
  - Not enough attention: distribution problem.
  - People see content but never visit the App Store: creative or positioning problem.
  - They start onboarding but never reach the paywall: onboarding problem.
  - They reach the paywall but don't buy: offer problem.
- More traffic into a broken funnel "just helps you lose faster."
- The paywall is a "lie detector". It shows whether the promise was compelling, onboarding built desire, value was understood and the offer made sense. A weak paywall rate does not automatically mean "redesign the paywall"; the lie may have started in the ad, the App Store page or onboarding.
- Downloads, paying and staying are three different signals. A free app with a million downloads can have zero product-market fit. Downloading proves curiosity, paying proves the promise was valuable enough to act on, staying proves the product delivered. Only paying and staying can support a business.
- Higher conversion can hide causality: a longer trial raises conversion but gives other campaigns, organic content and outside events more time to influence the user, so you lose the ability to tell what caused the conversion. "The best metric in isolation can still create a worse decision system."
- His closing principle: "Nobody is coming to identify the bottleneck for you." The operator's job is to see the business clearly, find the current constraint, pull the right lever, and repeat when the constraint moves.
- He says the founder's calendar should expose the current constraint. If distribution is broken, a product meeting won't help; if people click but don't pay, more impressions won't help; if the core feature fails, a new logo won't help.

chunks.heading: Consumer apps vs B2B SaaS, features and retention
chunks.text:
- Consumer apps are not tiny SaaS companies. They can reach massive audiences with relatively low switching costs, so acquisition is priority #1. B2B has fewer qualified buyers, painful implementation and higher trust costs, so reliability and retention come first. Both need both; the order of operations differs. "Stop importing B2B SaaS playbooks into consumer."
- Every new feature creates another place to break: marketing promise, App Store page, onboarding, paywall, support burden, retention loop and the number of things to diagnose. Earn the right to expand by making the core job undeniable first.
- Power users are often seasonal. A fitness user obsesses while training for an event then disappears; a budgeting user lives in the app while paying off debt. That doesn't mean the product failed. Before building another retention feature, ask whether the user's goal just became less urgent.
- The fastest retention gain is usually not a new feature. Find the action retained users already repeat and make it faster, clearer, more reliable and its result more valuable. "Users stay because the thing they came for keeps getting better."
- Loudest users aren't always the most important. Power users give useful, detailed feedback but asking for 40 settings and an advanced dashboard is not what most want. Listen to them, but build primarily for the quiet basic-user majority who want one outcome with minimal effort.
- Streaks, badges and challenges amplify value but don't create it. Build in this order: value, then repetition, then progress mechanic. If the core action is useless, "you're just gamifying disappointment."
- Community doesn't need to be permanent. A utility app doesn't need a feed, comments or followers. Community can exist around a high-intent window (a shared challenge, a small accountability group, a team goal with a clear start and finish) while the core product stays simple and individual.

chunks.heading: Freemium, email and winback
chunks.text:
- Freemium test: if you give away the feature that makes people download, is there another outcome they would confidently pay for? If yes, freemium may work. If you must invent six weak upgrades to justify the subscription, it probably won't. "Free should create demand for paid value. It should not eliminate the only reason to buy."
- Stop using email like a receipt printer (install confirmation, trial reminder, cancellation notice). Use it to teach users how to get value, introduce another use case, reconnect them to a goal and bring back someone whose timing changed. You paid to acquire the relationship; it doesn't disappear when the user closes the app.
- Winback should reconnect the user to the original dream outcome, not open with "WE MISS YOU" and a random discount. Ask: is the goal relevant again, did their context change, did the product improve where they got stuck? "Winback works when the reason to return is stronger than the reason they left."

chunks.heading: Influencer and creator marketing economics
chunks.text:
- A creator's fee is not their actual cost. Add time chasing replies, negotiating, revising content, rescheduling posts, fixing links, collecting analytics and managing usage rights. A lower-fee creator can cost more than a higher-fee one. Ask whether they can become a repeatable partner or you restart each month. "Creator CAC includes management bandwidth, so price it that way."
- Creator rates are set by brands outside your category. Your competitor for a creator may be a high-margin physical-product company that can pay far more for the same audience. A niche can have perfect fit and trusted creators and still be a terrible channel. Ask who else is bidding for their attention and what they can afford.
- Integration style depends on the product. If the product is instantly understood and the magic moment looks good on camera, let the creator weave it into normal content. If value needs context, subtle integration confuses the audience; use a direct problem-first explanation or demo. "Native is good. Confusing is not."
- Flat creator fees buy upside and variance. One breakout post gives asymmetric upside, but you pay full price when a post dies. Follower count isn't enough: you need realistic expected views, a read on performance volatility, and a price that works across many attempts, not the one outcome you daydream about.
- Creator outreach: the inbox preview is the first landing page. The recipient should immediately understand that (1) it's paid, (2) you chose them for a reason, (3) the ask is clear, (4) next steps are easy. If someone needs a call to understand the opportunity, you created friction before the relationship started.
- A creator spreadsheet is valuable because it exposes where the system fails:
  - Not enough replies: fix outreach or the list.
  - Creators agree but never post: fix onboarding, scheduling or incentives.
  - Posts go live but don't perform: fix selection, integration or angle.
  - Winners never renew: fix follow-up and deal structure.

chunks.heading: Execution, moats and process
chunks.text:
- The visible tactic is almost never the moat. People constantly copied Cal AI's influencer strategy and Jake didn't worry. The hard part was finding creators daily, sending outreach, negotiating, reviewing content, tracking delivery, renewing winners, cutting losers and repeating faster than everyone else. "Information is easy to copy, but sustained execution volume is not."
- Do manual work before automation. Run a process manually until you know which steps repeat, which exceptions matter, what good performance looks like, where people get stuck and which decisions need judgment. Then automate the predictable parts. Automating too early "just scales your own messy setup."
- Move fast on reversible decisions (test the angle, ship the landing page, try the creator, change onboarding). Legal, safety, financial and high-cost decisions deserve a higher threshold. Speed is a weapon when you know which mistakes you can survive.
- Be wary of anyone who turns your problem into a 15-step proprietary framework before looking at the basic numbers. Complexity can be real, or part of the pitch. "Real expertise usually compresses the problem into the few variables that actually matter."

chunks.heading: Team, hiring and founder dynamics
chunks.text:
- Hiring minimums differ by role. For an early marketing hire he often bets on a hungry person who learns fast and won't let the opportunity slip, since marketing has lots of surface area where reps, taste and effort compound. Technical work has a baseline motivation can't replace. Don't use one hiring rule for every function.
- Over-systemizing can lose ambitious people. Two early Cal AI marketing team members left after the work was systemized enough that it stopped challenging them. Pay keeps people comfortable but can't always keep an ambitious person engaged when learning stops. If your best people outgrow the work, create a new problem worth owning.
- Prefer complementary founders over identical "killers." The team needs different forms of leverage: someone who sees opportunities others miss, someone who reduces messy decisions to first principles, someone who can build almost anything, and someone who systemizes the work and gets it in front of people. "The team wins when the strengths multiply."
- Being a little successful can be more dangerous than being a beginner. After a small win, people stop taking feedback, assume the first win proved their worldview and protect the identity of being successful. The best operators eventually look like beginners again: curious, hardworking, open to being wrong.
- Understand luck. Separate what you controlled, earned, what others contributed, what happened at the perfect time, and what could have gone the other way. Crediting everything to your own brilliance means you'll try to repeat the wrong part.
- Money can't manufacture long-term interest. He spent years in management consulting earning more than ever and hated almost every day; at Cal AI he worked longer hours for almost no money and had more energy. If every week needs a new productivity system, the problem may be the thing you chose to work on.
- Reinvest after evidence, not ego. Early traction means the company may deserve more resources, not that you should act rich. Strengthen the product, upgrade the technical foundation, bring in great designers, pay for legal and financial help, fix what breaks at scale. "The lifestyle rewards can wait. The market window may not."

chunks.heading: AI as leverage for skilled operators
chunks.text:
- Give the same AI tool to a beginner and an elite operator and the elite operator usually gets more leverage: they know what to build, recognize weak output, know which detail matters, and connect results to distribution.
- "AI lowers the cost of execution. It does not remove the value of taste, context or reps." In many markets he expects AI to widen the gap between skilled and unskilled operators.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo synthesizes RevenueCat, Adapty and AppsFlyer research to argue consumer apps are easier to build but harder to win. AI moved the moat to distribution, brand, retention and experiment speed; first-session activation, channel ecosystems, web checkout tradeoffs and iOS vs Android differences decide who wins.

chunks.heading: Core thesis: AI moved the moat, it did not remove it
chunks.text:
- Jake says consumer apps have "never been easier to build AND harder to succeed."
- A founder can go from idea to working app faster and cheaper than ever. Features that took a team six months can now be copied in a few days.
- The moat now sits in everything around the product:
  - Distribution
  - Brand
  - Creator relationships
  - Proprietary data
  - Customer trust
  - Experiment velocity
  - Retention
- He keeps saying distribution matters more than product. He does not mean a terrible product can be marketed into success. He means a good product with no repeatable way to reach customers is "really just a side project waiting to be copied."
- Winners in 2026 build the fastest system for creating demand, proving value, and turning what they learn into the next thousand retained customers.

chunks.heading: Market shape: growing, but the middle is disappearing
chunks.text:
Figures Jake cites (RevenueCat, unless noted):
- About 14,700 new consumer apps launch every month, roughly 7X the 2022 rate.
- Only 17.3% of apps reach $1,000 in monthly revenue within two years, and just 4.6% reach $10,000.
- Consumer in-app spending hit $167 billion last year, and non-gaming apps passed gaming apps in revenue for the first time.
- Apps launched before 2020 still generate 69% of all app store subscription revenue.
- The top 25% of apps grew revenue by roughly 80% last year while the bottom 25% shrank by 33%.

His takeaway: more demand does not mean everybody wins. Operators with working systems take more of the market. Four questions to ask:
- Can you get someone's attention?
- Can you turn that attention into an install?
- Can you prove the app's value before they leave?
- Can you make the economics work well enough to do it again tomorrow?

chunks.heading: AI apps sell better than they retain
chunks.text:
- AI apps convert downloads to paid users roughly 20% better than non-AI apps and generate about 41% more revenue per payer.
- Annual AI subscriptions retain at 21.1% after one year versus 30.7% for non-AI apps.
- Jake's read: AI gets people interested but gives them no automatic reason to stay.
- Positioning rule: sell the outcome, not the technology. "Nobody wants an AI language app because it has a chatbot." They want to feel comfortable speaking Spanish before their trip to Spain.
- "AI is the mechanism, and the outcome is the real product."
- Stress test: if your app stops being interesting the second Apple, Google, or OpenAI ships the same feature, "you do not have an AI business."
- Diagnostic question: which part of your product gets stronger as AI models improve, rather than easier to replace?

chunks.heading: Organic and paid distribution do different jobs
chunks.text:
- AppsFlyer data he cites: paid installs drive only about 30% of non-gaming subscription revenue, and organic users generate 69% to 80% of installs depending on region.
- His framework: organic is the testing ground; paid is where you put spend behind winning concepts and formats for sustainable, predictable growth.
- Attribution trap: each scaling channel wants credit for the same customer. Judging channels in a vacuum instead of as one funnel ecosystem means you may cut something that helps the whole system convert.
- Winning apps do not look for one perfect channel. They build a multi-path system where every channel makes the next one convert better.
- Evaluate acquisition sources by which ones produce first renewals, not just cheap installs.

chunks.heading: The first session is the battleground
chunks.text:
- Retention keeps getting harder as new apps launch daily and attention spans shrink, so the first session cannot be a seven-screen product tour.
- It must answer three questions fast:
  1. Am I in the right place?
  2. Can this app solve the problem I'm experiencing?
  3. Why should I pay for it now?
- Best onboarding does not explain every feature. It gets the user to the magic moment, then presents the offer in the context of the result they just experienced.
- Paywall type (hard paywall, free trial, or freemium) depends on the product. "There is no universal best paywall setup. There is only the best access model for how quickly your product can prove itself."
- Metric to check: how long it takes a retained customer to reach the "aha" moment.

chunks.heading: Web checkout is another funnel, not free money
chunks.text:
- Big operators are adding web-to-app funnels, web subscriptions, and external checkout, to save platform fees and own more of the customer relationship.
- Counter-example: in a RevenueCat-reported Dipsea test, native in-app purchase produced 42% more initial conversions than an equivalent web checkout. The web flow saved fees but added friction that cost more revenue than the fees saved.
- His rule: "margin saved is not the same as revenue earned."
- Use web2app when customers need more education, personalization, pricing flexibility, or payment options before installing.
- Use native checkout when speed and trust matter more than the fee.
- Test by audience rather than forcing every customer down one path.

chunks.heading: iOS and Android are different businesses
chunks.text:
- By Day 35, iOS apps convert about 2.6% of downloads to paid versus 0.9% on Android. Once a trial starts, conversion rates are almost identical, so the gap is before the trial begins.
- His advice: the fix is not automatically a lower price. The problem may be the offer, payment method, onboarding, device performance, or trust required to start a trial.
- Android paid acquisition is growing fastest in markets like India and Latin America, while iOS still produces the majority of subscription revenue.
- Android needs its own customer behavior analysis, unit economics, and growth strategy. "Stop treating Android like an iOS version you remembered to launch later."

chunks.heading: Experiment velocity is the operating advantage
chunks.text:
- The best operators do not predict the market. They build a faster path to finding out when they are wrong.
- Adapty found bigger median lifts from testing localization, trial structure, plan duration, and the number of plans on the paywall than from price changes alone.
- He does not advocate running 100 random A/B tests. Test the biggest structural question first:
  - Who is the customer?
  - What promise gets their attention?
  - How quickly can they taste the dream outcome?
  - Which access model fits that experience?
  - Which channel brings customers who renew?
- The app that learns the answers faster reinvests faster, and that speed compounds.

chunks.heading: Jake's five-question funnel audit
chunks.text:
1. How long does it take a retained customer to hit an "aha" moment?
2. Which acquisition sources produce first renewals, not just cheap installs?
3. Where is the biggest drop between ad view, install, activation, payment, and renewal?
4. Which part of your product gets stronger as AI models improve instead of easier to replace?
5. What is the biggest structural test you can ship in the next two weeks?

- Do not rebuild the whole funnel at once. Find the weakest handoff, fix it, then move to the next.
- Closing line: "The consumer app market is not too crowded. It is just no longer forgiving."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo explains how to choose free trial length and whether to go freemium. Longer trials convert better because people forget to cancel, but shorter trials give clean install-to-revenue attribution when buying traffic through creators. Freemium only works when the free feature differs from the paid upsells.

chunks.heading: When Jake runs a free trial, and what it requires first
chunks.text:
- Jake says free trials fit any consumer app growth strategy, but only after "significant proof that people actually want your product and will pay for it."
- Trials can't compensate for a boring product that doesn't solve a real problem, bad marketing, or poor messaging.
- His starting recommendation, once an app has PMF, a product people pay for, and is ready to test trials, is a LONGER trial rather than a shorter one.
- A short trial only makes sense if everything around it holds up. Otherwise "all you did was shorten your trial and take a lower conversion rate for it." The conditions:
  - The app hits its magic moment in the first session.
  - Onboarding is optimized.
  - The paywall is optimized.
  - Traffic spend is high enough that attribution actually matters.

chunks.heading: Why longer trials convert better
chunks.text:
- Someone downloads the app, sees 14 days, figures they'll cancel later, and forgets.
- The trial turns into a subscription for at least a month. If you run ads, that helps liquidate some of the ad spend.
- Longer trials convert better because "you're banking on subscribers forgetting to cancel."
- With a 1 or 3 day trial the reaction is the opposite: users panic, go straight to settings, and cancel the same afternoon.
- He cites RevenueCat: 84% of 3-day trial cancellations happen on day 0 or day 1.

chunks.heading: Short trials as a price for attribution (Cal AI example)
chunks.text:
- At Cal AI, Jake ran 300+ creators at one time. Big promo days produced a massive spike in installs.
- With a 3-day trial, he could compare Monday's install spike to Thursday's revenue spike and attribute installs to a specific creator.
- With a 7-day trial, Monday's installs line up with the following Monday's revenue. By then four other creators have posted and one video may have gone viral, so credit can't be assigned.
- Every extra trial day adds variables between the install and the credit card charge.
- Attribution matters more than conversion rate, because it decides which creators to keep or cut.
- Two creators can drive identical installs and very different paying subscriptions. A non-U.S. audience converts far less than an American one because of lower disposable income.
- Without clean attribution he'd risk re-signing the wrong creator and pouring budget into an audience that would never pay for Cal AI.
- The real question, in his words, is "whether a few points of conversion are worth losing the ability to read your own channel." For Cal AI, "it wasn't close."

chunks.heading: Decision rule for trial length
chunks.text:
- Not paying for traffic: run the longer trial. There are no creators to attribute.
- Buying installs: shorten it. "You're not optimizing conversion at that point, you're buying signal, and trial length is what you pay for it."

chunks.heading: Freemium vs. paid: ask what people came in the door for
chunks.text:
- Jake treats the freemium question as the same logic as trial length, not an unrelated one.
- Old calorie-tracking apps drew users with their food databases. They could give the database away free and upsell barcode scanning, macros, and other premium add-ons. Users came for one thing and paid for four others they didn't know they wanted.
- People downloaded Cal AI for AI food scanning. That feature IS the product.
- Making it free would leave no second feature anyone would pay for: "a pile of users and no revenue."
- Rule: freemium works when there is a great baseline feature plus upsells on the backend. When the draw and the paid feature are the same thing, "freemium is just churn with extra steps."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake argues influencer marketing still works but CPMs have spiked across all creator tiers because everyone copied the Cal AI playbook, killing margins. He recommends shifting to UGC (not yet exhausted or overpriced), sourcing via SideShift or Trybe, and moving Q4 effort into organic since paid CPMs spike. He lists funnel prerequisites UGC needs to convert.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing didn't stop working, it stopped being cheap
chunks.text:
- Jake still says yes to "does influencer marketing work?", but the real question is whether you can still get a good deal on it. His answer as of August 2026 is "mostly no".
- Creator quality didn't drop. RPMs didn't drop either. The revenue side looks the same as when he was signing creator deals in 2024-25.
- What changed is CPMs, which "jumped waaaay up".
- His explanation: people saw profitable brands scaling with influencers (including his own operation) and decided influencer marketing was the move. Everyone now bids for the same creators, and the creators have caught on.
- His takeaway, in his words: "Influencer marketing didn't stop working. It just stopped being cheap."

chunks.heading: How creator pricing shifted: from mid-tier sweet spot to everyone overpriced
chunks.text:
- The old market had two distortions:
  - Giant brands overpaid at the top.
  - Small influencers overcharged companies with no influencer deal experience.
  - So the best viable option was mid-tier creators.
- Now every influencer is overpriced in general, including the "bottom of the barrel" creators. Jake says this is "killing margins like crazy".
- Concrete benchmark: his team retained 300+ creators at one time two years ago. He says they would not have been able to do that under today's pricing structure.
- He has an X thread on how to price influencer deals (linked in the post) for anyone who still wants to run them.

chunks.heading: Why Jake is looking hard at UGC right now
chunks.text:
- Three main distribution channels for consumer apps, as he frames them: paid ads, influencer deals, and UGC.
- UGC "hasn't been exhausted YET" and isn't overpriced yet.
- He compares UGC today to where influencer marketing sat a couple of years ago, "right before everyone started trying to copy the Cal AI playbook".
- He frames this as a window of opportunity that is likely to close as more people pile in.
- He points to an X article by @jammer3k on running a UGC program the right way (he notes it is not sponsored or affiliated).

chunks.heading: Sourcing UGC creators: SideShift and Trybe
chunks.text:
The hardest part of UGC is sourcing high quality creators. Jake's recommendations (he states he is not sponsored on either):

- **SideShift** for mass UGC campaigns
  - Has an abundance of creators.
  - Faster than a VA scrolling TikTok and Instagram all day.
- **Trybe** if you mainly run paid ads
  - Creators make the content with nothing paid upfront.
  - You run it as an ad, and the creator takes a percentage of the spend on the video they made.
  - You pay out only on performance.
- **Staffing**: one VA doing manual outreach on TikTok and Instagram (what Jake did himself), plus one VA searching SideShift or Trybe, gives the best odds of finding creators to work with.

chunks.heading: Q4 paid ads: don't try to outbid anyone
chunks.text:
- Meta and TikTok CPMs climb "through the roof" in Q4 because of Black Friday and Christmas. Every e-commerce brand fights over sales to finish the year strong.
- His advice for consumer apps: don't try to outbid anybody.
- Accept early that you won't scale insanely fast or profitably on paid in Q4, and move that time and energy into organic channels.
- This Q4 effect is a second reason, alongside the bloated influencer market, to prioritize UGC now.

chunks.heading: When UGC will not work: check your fit and funnel first
chunks.text:
Jake warns that you can source great creators, get the content made, and still wrongly blame the creators or format when it doesn't convert. UGC will fail if:

- You don't have solid marketing angles and scripts.
- Your product is hard to understand in 2-5 seconds.
- Your budget is too small to test enough before one of your videos goes viral.
- Your entire funnel isn't congruent.
- Your onboarding isn't optimized.
- Your paywall isn't optimized.

His verdict on those cases: "that's on you". He has a separate X article on onboarding and paywall optimization (linked in the post) for anyone who needs help there.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo argues founders sample feedback from the groups that talk (power users via behavior, complainers via support channels) while the silent majority generates most revenue. Using a mass-market gym analogy and Cal AI's Android launch, he says to build for the majority, simplify the first screen, and sanity-check requests with three numbers.

chunks.heading: Jake builds for the silent majority, not the loud minority
chunks.text:
- Jake argues founders are power users of their own product, and in consumer apps this is a costly bias. From the inside it just feels like caring about product quality.
- He says the second version of the mistake is the handful of users who are furious about a missing feature and ask for it repeatedly. In his view this is usually a misleading demand signal.
- His default is to ignore or delay the off-the-wall requests from users and put power-user projects on the backburner.
- He says to "always be building apps for the majority first, not the minority."
- Power users are die-hard fans and ambassadors who want the most out of the app, but they are a small share of those who open it.
- His rule for evaluating a feature: "this feature is the best thing we built" may be true, yet it can serve only about 5% of the people who will open the app tomorrow.

chunks.heading: The gym analogy: mass-market products are designed for the average user
chunks.text:
- Jake points to mass-marketed gyms (Planet Fitness, Crunch Fitness, Anytime Fitness), which follow a similar blueprint.
- The floor is about 80% cardio equipment, a section of muscle-isolation machines, and a few benches and squat racks.
- Most members are walking on a treadmill, because that is exercise to them and what they pay for.
- Only about 10% keep detailed workout logs and track every set, rep, weight and everything they eat.
- Building a commercial gym for that 10% would mean building a gym most members do not want to be in.
- His point: the biggest chains in the country make this call deliberately, so app founders should make it too.
- Most users of an app are basic users. They do not need or want all the features built for the few.

chunks.heading: Cal AI's Android mistake: a real number attached to the wrong population
chunks.text:
- Jake says Cal AI listened to the loud minority while scaling, and it went badly.
- The team built iOS first. Users then kept asking when Android was launching ("When's the Android app launching?", "Why isn't this on Android?", "We NEED this on Android.").
- On paper the logic looked airtight: Android is roughly 70% of global smartphone users. The team built it expecting the market to at least double.
- After launch, the app "MAYBE grew 10%."
- His explanation:
  - iPhone users are predominantly in the U.S.
  - Android users make up most of the rest of the world, where disposable income is lower and paying for an app is much less culturally normal.
  - People outside the US who do have money to spend on apps are, by and large, already carrying an iPhone.
- His conclusion: "the 70% was never addressable. It was a real number attached to the wrong population."
- Lesson: check whether a big addressable-market statistic maps to people who actually pay before building for it.

chunks.heading: Why founders hear the wrong people: you only sample from the group that talks
chunks.text:
- Power users talk to you through behavior. They are in the app constantly, hit every corner, and their usage shows up loudest in analytics. You build for what you see, and what you see is them.
- Complainers talk through feedback channels: endless comments, a full support inbox, reviews. You hear them, so you build for them too.
- The roughly 95% silent majority is silent in both directions. They do not leave feature requests and do not show up as power sessions. They open the app, get what they came for or do not, and stay or leave quietly.
- Jake says the silent majority is also "almost all of your revenue."
- His warning: your loudest signals and your biggest revenue segment are, 99% of the time, two different groups of people.

chunks.heading: Two things to do this week: simplify the first screen and score requests before building
chunks.text:
1. Audit the first screen:
   - Open the app and count how many elements on the first screen serve fewer than 10% of users.
   - Move every one of them a tap or layer deeper, and simplify everything.
2. Before building the next thing everybody is asking for, write down three numbers:
   - How many people actually asked.
   - What share of them would pay for it.
   - What share of the silent majority would ever touch it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo says Cal AI's rise to #1 in Health & Fitness and $50M ARR in eighteen months owed a lot to luck, not a replicable process. His practical advice: pay for great talent via headhunters, sell candidates hard, give generous equity, and hire for availability and ability to learn over experience.

chunks.heading: Luck, not a template: Jake's view on how Cal AI's founding team came together
chunks.text:
- Jake's most common founder question is how to find a group like the four Cal AI founders (cracked co-founders, CEO, COO, CTO, designers, devs).
- The team of four got along through roughly two and a half years of intense stress. Two were still in high school when they started, and Henry's mom had to co-sign for the company bank account.
- Cal AI went from nothing to #1 in Health & Fitness and $50M ARR in eighteen months, then the company was sold.
- His answer is blunt: "We got extremely lucky." He calls that kind of team "a freak thing" that does not happen repeatedly, even compared with something like the PayPal mafia.
- He says he has "watched enough founding teams up close now" to know how unusual it was.

chunks.heading: Hard work and smarts increase surface area for luck
chunks.text:
- Jake is explicitly not saying outcomes are random.
- He used to believe the hardest working and smartest people win. He no longer does, because "often the luckiest people win."
- Working hard and being smart "just increases your surface area for luck." He calls that real and most of what a founder can control.
- Luck can still happen without a big surface area, and "people do all the time."
- He says pretending otherwise is "a lie that makes everyone reading it feel worse about themselves."

chunks.heading: Why Cal AI's origin story is not a template
chunks.text:
- Jake argues people read the origin story as something engineered, which it never was.
- The chain of events that led him to Zach Yadegari and Cal AI:
  - A YouTube video his cousin sent him about Tabs Chocolate.
  - That led him to hear Oliver Brocato talk about internet money and his businesses.
  - He followed Oliver on X and happened to be scrolling when Oliver tweeted that he needed a COO.
  - He cold DMed Oliver, never expecting a response.
  - Oliver saw it and asked to jump on a call.
  - Jake started moonlighting for Oliver at Studybuddy.
  - Zach happened to be interning at Studybuddy too.
- His takeaway: if you are waiting to assemble a once-in-a-lifetime, "Avengers style" co-founder group who are brilliant, get along, and are available, "you might die waiting."

chunks.heading: Great people are expensive, hard to find, and already have options
chunks.text:
- Jake's core hiring principle: "You have to pay to play."
- He compares cheap great talent to "a gold watch on the beach," and says once you find it, it only gets more expensive over time.
- Great candidates usually do not need you. They already have a solid job, and you are asking them to risk joining something that might not exist in a year.
- So even after you get a few solid candidates, you have to sell them hard on why they should work with you.

chunks.heading: Use a headhunter for vetted talent
chunks.text:
- For finding vetted top talent fast, Jake recommends a headhunter.
- Fees usually run around 20% of first-year salary, which he says is "100% worth it."
- His reasoning: sourcing great talent is mind-numbing work, and most founders have not hired enough people to be good at it.
- When someone says they will not pay that fee, he tells them they will not get great talent.

chunks.heading: Be generous with equity
chunks.text:
- If you are running a startup, Jake says to be prepared to be generous with equity.
- This applies especially when someone has the intangibles you are looking for.

chunks.heading: Hire for availability and ability to learn, not experience alone
chunks.text:
- Jake does not hire for experience alone. He hires for availability and for whether someone can and wants to learn.
- The two questions he asks: "Is this person actually here, and can they figure out something they do not currently know?"
- He says those two things predict more than any resume he has glanced over.
- Experience can work against you. An experienced hire arrives certain about how they like to do things, and that way is often not compatible with, or best for, what the company needs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo distills eight tactics from the Cal AI creator-marketing playbook: price deals off average views, decide between soft and hard sell, target oversupplied creator niches, vet creators in 20 seconds, write short outreach, pay upfront, and repeat winning formats. He closes with the point that volume and relentless work, not a secret unlock, drove the results.

chunks.heading: Pricing creator deals off average views, not hope
chunks.text:
- Jake says a creator's floor has to be their average views. When he looks at a creator's page, the worst-performing videos are "almost every time" the sponsored posts, because the brand pushed the creator away from what they normally make.
- At Cal AI, every deal was priced off the creator's average views. He tells others to do the same.
- Management cost is the same regardless of creator size. A creator doing 20k views and one doing a million cost identical time: contracts, scheduling, review, comments, renewal and payment. Everyone has a bandwidth ceiling, so he spends his on the bigger creators.

chunks.heading: Deciding between a seamless integration and a hard sell
chunks.text:
Two questions decide how hard the promo needs to push:

1. Is the product easy to understand?
2. Does it have a magic moment?

- If both are yes, do a seamless integration and let the product carry the promo.
- If either is missing, you need a hard sell.
- Cal AI was a yes to both. Everybody already knew what calorie tracking was, and in early 2024 "pointing a phone at a plate and getting calories in seconds stopped people in their tracks."

chunks.heading: Picking a niche with too many creators
chunks.text:
- Fitness worked partly because there are far more fitness creators than brands trying to work with them.
- That supply mismatch gets you cheaper deals to start and lets you figure out which creators fit your brand.
- The demographic Jake would target now is college kids: huge supply, almost no brands that know how to work with them, "nothing but time and no money." They'll take a rate "a working professional would laugh at."

chunks.heading: The 20-second creator screening test
chunks.text:
After reviewing over 10,000 creator profiles, Jake checks four things quickly:

- Do they clear 25k views a video?
- Are the comments real people sharing opinions, or just fire emojis?
- Are there reply threads under those comments?
- Do they have a parasocial relationship with their audience?

His reasoning: real comments usually mean a cult following. Reply threads mean the audience talks to each other, not just to the creator. That is a community, and "communities convert better than anything else."

chunks.heading: Cold outreach to creators
chunks.text:
- Creators get around a hundred DMs a day and open maybe ten. They decide off the preview line before opening the message.
- Don't open with your life story or "I'm a bootstrapped founder." Open with "paid promo" or something that answers "What's in it for me?"
- Keep the message short enough to answer in one line.
- Whether to name a price depends on the creator. A college kid who has never done a deal sees $100 and takes it. A creator with fifty brand deals behind her will anchor against you, so let her start the money conversation.

chunks.heading: Pay creators 100% upfront
chunks.text:
- Almost every experienced creator has been burned by a brand that didn't pay. That is the number one reason they say no, and paying upfront removes their biggest fear of getting ripped off.
- It also solved a personal problem for Jake. He is 30 and looks young, and he could see creators on calls thinking "this kid can't afford me." Saying he pays upfront ends that conversation before it starts.

chunks.heading: Find a winning format, then stop being creative
chunks.text:
- Cal AI found one format that worked with one fitness creator, then signed as many fitness creators as possible to make the exact same video.
- While that ran, a separate team tested whether the format carried into other niches.
- His rule: "Find it, copy it, run it until it dies. Then go find the next one."

chunks.heading: Volume is the only unlock
chunks.text:
- Jake says none of the tactics matter if you won't do the volume. People ask for the secret Cal AI scaling unlock, and he says there isn't one.
- He worked from 6am to midnight for two years, often falling asleep with the laptop in bed, and kept going the next morning.
- His view is that copycat Cal AI apps didn't beat Cal AI because they weren't willing to work that hard. He adds he isn't saying you have to do that, but if you're asking whether you're working hard enough, "you already know the answer."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake curates seven mobile app and subscription operators worth studying instead of courses or YouTube. He highlights concrete growth lessons: content-led distribution, ASO concentration on a few keywords, portfolio-of-simple-apps systems, and solo AI-assisted building.

chunks.heading: Why founders should learn from operators, not courses
chunks.text:
Jake's core argument: anyone trying to build a profitable app has two options. One is to spend hundreds of hours researching ideas and bingeing coding and marketing tutorials, then quit because they don't know where to start or whose advice to trust. The other is to study people "actually in the arena", meaning those shipping apps, running profitable companies and posting what works in real time. He says following a few of these operators is "more valuable than any course or YouTube video you'll consume."

His practical recommendation: pick any two of the seven operators he lists, read everything they've published, and you'll know more about building a profitable app than 95% of people calling themselves founders. His framing is that the barrier to building has never been lower, and the barrier to learning from the right people has just dropped too.

chunks.heading: Eric Seufert: mobile advertising and paid acquisition economics
chunks.text:
Jake recommends Eric Seufert as the "marketing economist". Seufert ran growth at Wooga and Rovio (the Angry Birds studio), wrote the book *Freemium Economics*, and built and sold a marketing analytics company.

- His blog Mobile Dev Memo explains how mobile advertising actually works after the privacy changes.
- Jake points to him for founders asking why their paid acquisition isn't converting and what to do instead.
- Jake calls him one of the deepest thinkers in the space on this topic.

chunks.heading: Jacob Eiting: pricing, paywalls and subscription conversion
chunks.text:
Jake calls Jacob Eiting "the subscription whisperer". Eiting is founder/CEO of RevenueCat, which powers in-app subscriptions for 30,000+ apps. That gives him a view of what is making money across the whole App Store.

- Jake says to listen to him on pricing, paywalls and conversion because he is "reading from the largest subscription dataset on earth."
- Distribution lesson Jake highlights: Eiting grew RevenueCat from $400/month to $2M ARR by writing content that answered the exact questions developers were Googling. Jake calls this "an elite distribution lesson in itself."

chunks.heading: David Barnard and Adam Lyttle: indie app playbooks and portfolio systems
chunks.text:
**David Barnard, the indie veteran.** Barnard has been building apps since the App Store launched in 2008. He has shipped 30+ projects, sold four, and survived every algorithm shift.

- He is RevenueCat's Growth Advocate and hosts the Sub Club podcast, where he extracts tactical playbooks from the founders behind big apps.
- Jake values his war stories, including launches that flopped badly and how to actually A/B test.

**Adam Lyttle, the portfolio machine.** Lyttle went from $200K in debt to a reported $800K+ across a portfolio of 50+ simple apps. Jake sees this as proof that you don't need to build the next Instagram to win.

- His approach is a repeatable system: find a niche, build simply, optimize for App Store discovery, repeat.
- He posts ASO tricks, rapid-build sprints and revenue numbers openly.
- Jake calls him the most actionable follow on the list for a solo builder.

chunks.heading: Thomas Petit: App Store Optimization and Apple Search Ads
chunks.text:
Jake calls Thomas Petit "the distribution mechanic". Petit is an independent growth advisor who has consulted for 20+ apps including Deezer and Babbel, and won the 2022 App Growth Award for contribution to the community.

- Jake values him as someone who tells hard truths others won't.
- Example Jake cites: even when you target hundreds of keywords in Apple Search Ads, most of your downloads come from just five to ten of them.
- Jake's pointer: if App Store Optimization and paid search are your bottleneck, Petit is the operator to study.

chunks.heading: Josh Mohrer: solo-building an AI app with AI tools
chunks.text:
Jake describes Josh Mohrer as "the zero-to-code solo founder". Mohrer helped build Uber's New York operation from zero to billions in revenue. He then taught himself to code using ChatGPT and solo-built Wave AI to $4M ARR in eight months, with no employees or co-founder.

- Jake sees him as living proof of the new "solopreneur" reality, where one person with AI tools and business sense can build a real company.
- Jake says to follow him for the playbook on shipping an AI app with a tiny team.

chunks.heading: Sylvain Gauchet: onboarding and early user experience
chunks.text:
Jake calls Sylvain Gauchet "the insight miner". Gauchet runs growth at Babbel and distills tactical insights from hundreds of growth podcasts, webinars and talks into his Growth Gems newsletter.

- His specialty is onboarding and the early user experience, which Jake calls "the exact moments that determine whether someone churns or becomes a paying subscriber."
- Jake's framing: he is a curated filter that turns thousands of hours of content into "the 5% that actually moves revenue."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: App founders echo-chamber on other app founders, but ecom brands have battle-tested retention playbooks because rising CAC forces them to preserve every customer. Jake says to take ecom principles (default subscription, lifecycle email, preservation vs generation) and translate them into app versions like paywall defaults and pause-instead-of-cancel.

chunks.heading: Ecom brands are the best source of app retention ideas
chunks.text:
Jake argues app founders sit in an echo chamber of other app founders on X and LinkedIn, especially on retention. He says the most aggressive retention playbooks are in ecommerce, and apps should copy them and adapt the principles.

- Ecom is "a knife fight": CPMs and CAC keep climbing and every brand sells a version of the same product, so every funnel step matters.
- He expects apps to head to the same place: paid acquisition gets too expensive to waste a single customer.
- He quotes "Good artists copy, great artists steal" and says there is a lot worth stealing in ecom.
- Study how big ecom brands run their emails after you buy from them: welcome flow, winback flow, upsell and cross-sell emails.
- His method: follow a few DTC operators, sign up for their subscriptions, then try to cancel and screenshot every step. He says this yields more retention ideas than hours on YouTube.

chunks.heading: AG1: make the subscription the default
chunks.text:
Jake cites a YouTube video about changes AG1 made to its main product page that raised LTV and average order value.

- The only option above the fold is the subscription button, so it looks like the only way to buy.
- The one-time purchase option appears only if you scroll down.
- His app translation: make the annual plan the hero of the paywall.
- He asks founders: is the annual plan the obvious default, or are you showing three plans side by side and "asking a stranger to do math"?

chunks.heading: Olipop: treat subscription as a later stage in the relationship
chunks.text:
Jake describes Eli Weiss (@eliweisss), who ran CX and retention at Olipop and Jones Road, as taking the opposite approach to AG1.

- Olipop doesn't default anyone into a subscription and doesn't market it to first-time buyers.
- Eli treats the subscription as a stage the customer opts into once they already love the product.
- His rule of thumb, as Jake relays it: remove the friction first, then add flexibility (skip a delivery, swap a flavor, change the cadence, anything that keeps someone from hitting cancel).
- Jake says Eli grew Olipop's subscriptions 3x in a year this way.
- Jake's conclusion on AG1 vs Olipop: both are right. "AG1 wins the first sale. Olipop wins the hundredth." The move is stealing insights from both.

chunks.heading: Generation vs preservation, and cutting churn
chunks.text:
Jake cites Nick Shackelford (@iamshackelford), co-founder of BREZ and Structured, who has managed hundreds of millions in ad spend.

- Nick's team reduced BREZ's subscription churn from 24% to 17% and is chasing sub-5%.
- He splits the business into two buckets: generation (ads and content) and preservation (email, community, and keeping the customers you already paid for).
- Jake's observation: most app founders he talks to have a full team on generation and "one intern fumbling around" on keeping customers from leaving.

chunks.heading: Translating ecom tactics into app versions
chunks.text:
Jake says ecom tactics don't translate 1:1 (you can't, or shouldn't, ship a free t-shirt for subscribing to a single-use utility app, and you can't put a "subscribe and save 20%" badge on an App Store listing). The work is to take the principle and find the app version.

- Default the subscription becomes: make the annual plan the hero of your paywall.
- Reorder reminder (for a product that lasts 30 days) becomes: a push notification right before the habit breaks.
- Cancellation save offer becomes: "pause instead of cancel" in the manage-subscription flow.
- Unboxing experience becomes: the first 10 seconds in the app.
- Also borrow from ecom email: welcome, winback, upsell and cross-sell flows from brands you've bought from.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo ranks influencer tiers by conversion value, drawing on his experience at Cal AI and 10,000+ evaluated influencers. Mid-level creators are the best bet because deals still matter to them and audience trust is intact, while celebrities have no borrowed trust left to sell. He stresses per-deal effort and volume pipelines.

chunks.heading: Why creator tier decides influencer ROI
chunks.text: Jake says influencer marketing lives or dies on two tasks done well: picking the right niche, and identifying creators in that niche whose audiences are "primed for conversion." Fail at either and a brand burns budget, then claims the channel "doesn't work for them." His cheat sheet ranks creator tiers so operators can research the right partners first and avoid spreading cash in every direction "just to see what sticks." His ranking comes from evaluating over 10,000 influencers and signing too many creators that flopped.

chunks.heading: S tier: mid-level creators are where the math works
chunks.text:
- Big enough for real reach, small enough that your deal still matters to them.
- Pricing stays reasonable because nobody fights over them: giant brands chase celebrities and small brands chase micro-influencers.
- Their audience still sees them as relatable, so the trust being paid for is intact.
- At Cal AI, the most profitable deals usually came from this level, and the winners paid for every deal that didn't hit.
- Caveat: you still have to run enough deals in this category to find your winning formula.

chunks.heading: A tier: micro-influencers are a volume play
chunks.text:
- A creator with 30,000 followers feels like a friend to their audience, so a plug lands as a recommendation rather than an ad.
- They are cheaper and still convert, but no single micro-influencer deal will blow up downloads.
- The tier only works with a pipeline that signs and manages dozens of creators without the operator spending hours on logistics.

chunks.heading: B tier: nano-influencers are risky because per-deal work is fixed
chunks.text:
- The work to close a deal is the same whether the creator has 7,000 or 300,000 followers: outreach, negotiation, contracts, reviews, and making sure posts go live.
- At nano scale, deals may only break even or leave you in a small hole.
- A cult-like audience can still lose money, so pick carefully.
- His rule: if you can't get this tier down to near-zero effort per deal, skip it.

chunks.heading: C tier: big creators charge for reach, and reach alone rarely converts
chunks.text:
- Audiences know big creators do brand deals, so trust erodes as the paid partnership becomes visible.
- You pay premium prices for reach, which usually doesn't convert on its own.
- Jake's team broke this rule twice at Cal AI on very large bets that paid off, but he says that is not the norm.
- Signing someone at this level gives a "dopamine hit" but is often "an expensive way to feel important."

chunks.heading: F tier: celebrities have no borrowed trust left
chunks.text:
- Jake's framing: "The entire product in influencer marketing is borrowed trust."
- Everyone knows a celebrity post is an ad, and their audience follows them for entertainment, not for recommendations on improving their lives.
- You pay the most where the key lever, real trust, is absent.

chunks.heading: Checklist before wiring money
chunks.text:
- Know what you are paying for and whether it fits your current goals and revenue.
- Mid-tier creators worked best for Cal AI, but you still have to evaluate the quality of each influencer's audience yourself.
- Plan for volume: run enough mid-tier and micro deals to find the winners, and build a low-effort process for contracts, reviews and post tracking.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo argues that a frictionless app funnel depends on congruent messaging from top-of-funnel content through store page, onboarding and paywall. He borrows the native-ad funnel model, explains why one killer feature simplifies angles, and gives three benchmarks that diagnose which funnel step is broken.

chunks.heading: Congruency is the core principle of a high-converting app funnel
chunks.text:
- Jake tells almost every app founder he consults with: "Your funnel needs to be as frictionless as possible."
- The customer should feel like they are "effortlessly sliding down a slippery slope until they hit your paywall."
- The only way that happens is if every part of the funnel is congruent. His shorthand: "Congruency > everything else."
- Every screen after the first touchpoint either confirms or contradicts the story the prospect is building in their head about the solution. Confirm it enough times and they buy.

chunks.heading: Native ad funnels as the model of congruency
chunks.text:
Jake calls the marketers behind native ad funnels "masters of congruency." The sequence:

1. A user scrolls a news or sports site and sees a headline that grabs attention.
2. They click something that doesn't look like an ad.
3. It leads to a health quiz or an article that teaches them about a problem they didn't know they had.
4. They spend real time (10-15 minutes) answering questions and reading about why the thing they worry about happens.
5. Only then does a product appear. By then it doesn't feel like a pitch, it feels like the answer to a problem they likely have.

- These funnels work because the story and the messaging work together seamlessly.
- The counterexample: send native ad clicks straight to a product page and you are asking cold traffic to pay for a solution to a problem they may not realize they have.

chunks.heading: Applying congruency to an app funnel
chunks.text:
- Once you have identified winning angles for your product, top-of-funnel content (paid or organic) must use the same language and highlight a pain point or desired outcome.
- Every later stage must carry the same messaging all the way to the paywall: the app store page, or web2app funnel pages, then onboarding, then the paywall.
- The full path to keep consistent: content (paid or organic), store page, onboarding, paywall.

chunks.heading: Focus on one killer feature to simplify your angles
chunks.text:
- Jake says this is another reason Cal AI focused on "one killer feature" rather than five mediocre ones.
- One feature simplifies the marketing angles used to promote the product.
- His framing: "Give your potential customers one idea to hold onto to survive the trip from a creator's video or ad all the way to your paywall."

chunks.heading: Funnel benchmarks that show where congruency breaks
chunks.text:
Jake's diagnostic thresholds, each mapping a weak metric to the two stages that disagree:

| Benchmark | What it means |
|---|---|
| Under 5 downloads per 1,000 views | Your creative and your store page disagree |
| Under 75% paywall rate | Your store page and your onboarding disagree |
| Under 10% paywall conversion | Your onboarding and your offer disagree |

- His conclusion: "stop blindly optimizing steps and start auditing every step of your funnel."

chunks.heading: The funnel audit exercise
chunks.text:
- Run through your own funnel "like a stranger" in one sitting this week: content (paid or organic), store page, onboarding, paywall.
- If it doesn't flow seamlessly end to end, find the fixes and watch what happens to your dashboard.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake Castillo explains why six years of "discipline problems" in consulting were really a motivation mismatch. He splits operators into mercenaries (money-driven) and missionaries (need to care about the thing) and gives seven questions to ask before committing to a project, so you don't burn two years operating as the wrong type.

chunks.heading: Missionaries need to care about the thing itself; mercenaries need only the payoff
chunks.text:
- Jake frames people (and operators) as either mercenaries or missionaries, and says this is a motivation split, not a discipline split.
- **Mercenary:** wants to make as much money as possible, as fast as possible, and is honest about it. Can work on something "genuinely boring for years and be completely fine," because "the dollar signs trigger the dopamine hits to keep them stimulated and on task."
- Jake calls this "a real, legitimate, and extremely effective way to operate." He says some of the best operators he knows are mercenaries and "will out-earn almost everyone."
- **Missionary:** needs to care about the thing itself. Not in a precious way; they just can't sustain effort on something they think is pointless.
- Failure mode: put a missionary on a boring product with great margins and they quit around month four, can't explain why, and feel like a flake.

chunks.heading: Six years of "I need more discipline" was really a motivation mismatch
chunks.text:
- After USC, Jake worked in management consulting with a two-hour train commute each way into LA, every day. He was paid what he thought was good money.
- He couldn't focus on work that bored him. Performance conversations repeated: "You lack attention to detail," "You seem unmotivated," and a proposed performance improvement plan.
- His story was that he needed better systems and routines. Meanwhile, colleagues three desks away did the same work (with "god awful slide decks"), liked it, and were moving up.
- His realization: those people weren't more disciplined. They were mercenaries in a mercenary's job and thriving. He was a missionary in a mercenary's job, "blaming myself for it, and calling the mismatch a character flaw."
- Takeaway: "I spent six years thinking I needed more discipline, when really I just needed different goals that mattered."

chunks.heading: Proof: the attention-to-detail problem vanished once the work was his
chunks.text:
- Two days after Jake quit consulting, Zach Yadegari called and asked him to work on Cal AI.
- For the first time in his adult working life, he was working on something "actually mine and meaningful."
- Passion did not make it easy. Building and scaling Cal AI was "the hardest two years of my life": twenty-hour days, no weekends, no income to speak of, an empty bank account, and a fiancée watching him disappear into a laptop.
- Yet "the attention to detail problem never came up again." What six years of performance reviews and discipline couldn't fix "evaporated the moment the work was mine and mattered to me."

chunks.heading: Ask the identity question before the market question
chunks.text:
- Most people pick what to build by looking at markets: where the money is, where growth potential is, which niches are underserved. Jake says those are good questions and you should ask them.
- But ask the identity question first, "because it determines whether you'll still be putting in the necessary hours at fourteen months in."
- **If you're a mercenary:** find the boring, high-margin thing and grind it out. "Don't let anyone tell you that you need to be passionate about accounting software."
- **If you're a missionary:** take the identity question seriously, because around month eight, when numbers are flat and the work stops being fun, you'll need something to hold onto.
- The goal isn't to become one or the other. It's to stop picking as one and operating as the other, "the version where you burn two years and call yourself lazy at the end of it."

chunks.heading: Seven questions to ask before committing to a project
chunks.text:
1. The last time you worked hard on something with no money attached, what was it? That's the missionary signal and "the most reliable data you have."
2. If this product made $30,000 a month forever and never grew past that, would you still want to run it in three years?
3. When you imagine the win, do you picture your bank account or the thing existing in the world? No wrong answer, but there is a true one.
4. What's the boring middle of this business (support tickets, ad reviews, contracts, reconciliation)? Picture doing that specific task three hours a day for a year.
5. Have you ever quit something that was working? What was actually going on? That pattern will repeat, so plan for it rather than be surprised.
6. Who are you trying to prove something to, and will they notice? Know the honest answer before spending two years on it.
7. What would a mercenary version of you say about this idea, and a missionary version? Which one is doing the talking right now?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake argues founders who say their app isn't growing usually can't name four core numbers: content/ad views, App Store impressions, paywall rate, and paywall conversion. Each metric points to a specific lever (traffic, message, or product), so you fix the furthest-off one instead of guessing. He shares Cal AI's benchmark targets.

chunks.heading: The three-stage diagnostic: views, downloads, paywall
chunks.text:
Jake argues that most founders who say "my app isn't growing" cannot name the numbers that show why. He says he asks every founder whether they know four metrics, and "very few" can recite all four:

1. Views generated by content and ads
2. Impressions on the App Store page
3. Paywall rate: the % of downloads that actually reach the paywall
4. Paywall conversion rate

Once you have these numbers, he says, "you know exactly which lever to pull." Two questions explain every one of the 300+ influencer deals he signed on the way to $50M ARR at Cal AI:

- Did the views turn into downloads?
- Did the downloads turn into paying users?

He says follower counts, likes and how good the video looked "never made the list."

chunks.heading: Cal AI benchmark targets
chunks.text:
Jake lists the targets his team aimed for at Cal AI:

- **View to download:** 5 downloads per 1,000 views (0.5%)
- **Paywall rate:** 75%+ of downloads reach the paywall
- **Paywall conversion:** 10%

His claim: hit these three consistently and "you will not have a user acquisition problem."

chunks.heading: Diagnosing which problem you actually have
chunks.text:
Jake maps each weak metric to one kind of problem, so you know what to fix before spending money:

- **Views are low:** a traffic problem. Get more eyeballs. Post more, sign more creators, or run ads if you have the capital.
- **Views are high but downloads are weak:** a message problem, or a demand problem. People saw the content and didn't care. Either the hook is wrong or nobody wants what you are selling.
- **Downloads are strong but conversion is weak:** a product problem. Look at onboarding and the paywall first, and see where people drop off in the flow.

chunks.heading: Fixing the wrong thing
chunks.text:
Jake says founders "love fixing the wrong thing." Two examples he has seen:

- People rebuilding a paywall when the real issue was that they needed more traffic.
- People pouring money into creators when half their users never made it to the paywall.

He says both feel productive but neither changes revenue. This is why he wants the numbers pulled before anyone spends on a fix.

chunks.heading: Keep the measurement stack simple
chunks.text: Jake warns founders to be wary of anyone who makes this sound complicated, such as "a full attribution stack, a 40-slide audit, and a 90-day retainer." In his view that is usually someone trying to sell a service. He says you can usually start with the four metrics above and resolve the issue.

chunks.heading: What to do this week
chunks.text:
Jake's instruction for a struggling app:

- Pull the four numbers this week.
- Whichever one is furthest off from the targets is your job for the next month.
- Everything else waits.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jake argues that AI makes people lazier and less able to think, so the way to beat competitors is to protect your own critical thinking. He recommends a 30-day, one-hour-a-day deliberate practice sprint on a skill you fear or are bad at, drawing on The First 20 Hours and Michael Smoak's 30-day video challenge.

chunks.heading: Critical thinking is the one skill AI can't replace, and Jake treats it as something to practice and protect
chunks.text:
- Jake describes AI as probably the greatest technological advancement in human history, and says he is "as AI-pilled as they come."
- He also says using it has made him "dumber to a degree." It can give a feeling of being more productive while he wastes time prompting AI for something he could have "cranked out in 20 mins myself."
- His main takeaway: "you need to practice and protect your ability to think critically at all costs."
- He argues that having original thoughts and articulating them intelligently may be the most important skill to master going forward.
- Evidence he points to for the value of human thinking: people still buy physical books, go to TED talks, and pay financial advisors.
- He notes that as everyone offloads thinking to chatbots, it has never been easier to stand out in the traditional job market.

chunks.heading: Beating competitors in any sector with one month of deep learning
chunks.text:
- Jake claims you can use AI to your advantage to beat out competition "in ANY sector in just 30 days," though "maybe not the way you're expecting."
- The edge is not more AI output. It is that most people are offloading their thinking, so one person who locks in for a month of real, intense learning can pull ahead.
- This applies to any high-income skill: understanding distribution for apps, email marketing, creating ads, or even learning guitar.
- He expects you to be bad at first and says that is the point: "You're going to suck at it at first, but that's the point."

chunks.heading: The First 20 Hours: why 10,000 hours is not required
chunks.text:
- Jake recommends *The First 20 Hours* by Josh Kaufman for standing out in any crowded market (he says it is not sponsored, and that reading summaries is fine).
- Kaufman's main thesis, as Jake relays it, challenges the idea that you need 10,000 hours to truly master a skill.
- Jake's takeaway is that a short, focused block of effort can "catapult yourself into a whole new realm of possibilities."

chunks.heading: "Where you fear is, there your task is": using fear as a signal for what to work on
chunks.text:
- Jake quotes Carl Jung: "Where you fear is, there your task is."
- He applies it when stuck on a task or dreading trying something new, knowing he will be bad at it.
- Example he cites: Michael Smoak (HigherUp Wellness on Instagram) was terrified of public speaking and making social media content about 3 years ago, so he forced himself into a 30-day challenge of recording one 60-second video per day.
- Three years later, Smoak has a multi-million-follower audience and has inspired over 100,000 people to complete the same 30-day public speaking challenge.

chunks.heading: Jake's 30-day challenge: the step-by-step protocol
chunks.text:
1. Pick up Josh Kaufman's book, or read summaries of it.
2. Write down what has been stressing you out or making you anxious over the last 30 days.
3. Lock yourself in a room for an hour every day for a month and "DO THE WORK."
4. Don't offload all your critical thinking to AI.

- He asks readers to email him after 30 days with what they were struggling with, what they did to overcome it, and where they are now.
- The core mechanic is a small, fixed daily time block (one hour, or one 60-second video in Smoak's case) aimed at the specific thing that scares or stresses you, repeated for 30 days.

chunks.heading: Working with Jake
chunks.text:
- Jake writes the Operator's Notebook newsletter, which he describes here as a "random Saturday thought dump," and offers 1:1 calls booked through Intro.
- He shares content on X and LinkedIn.
